title: DBRAG: Multi-Table Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Complex Database Queries
text: To enable scalable retrieval of multiple relevant tables while addressing (R1), we decompose the retriever into a two-step process. First, an efficient encoder is used to perform coarse-grained ranking, identifying a broad subset of top-K tables from the corpus. Then, an LLM is utilized to conduct finegrained reranking of these top-K tables to ensure higher precision in relevance and to identify the top-Mtables to formR q. Table Index: Coarse-grained Ranking.We employ an efficient encoder fenc to embed the coarsegrained summary of each table, which primarily consists of the table name, schema, and randomly sampled rows. For each tableti, we form itscoarsegrained table summaryas follows: si ={t Name i , t Schema i , t RandomRows i }, and compute its embedding ei =f enc(si). The query q is embedded as q=f enc(q), and tables are ranked by the cosine similarity between q and ei. The top- K tables constitute the coarse-rank candidate setCq.

title: DBRAG: Multi-Table Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Complex Database Queries
text: The top- K tables constitute the coarse-rank candidate setCq. Since these embeddings are independent of the query, they can be precomputed and stored in aTable Index. Row Index: Context Retrieval.To further enrich the candidate setCq, we augment each table with query-relevant row information. This process involves building a row embedding index by encoding each row in the database and storing it in a precomputedRow Index. Specifically, for each row r with column names c1, c2, . . . , cn and corresponding cell values v1, v2, . . . , vn, we form a row summary sr ={c 1, v1, c2, v2, . . . , cn, vn}, and compute its embedding ase r =f enc(sr). Adding the row context is crucial in DBRAG, as it enhances the system’s understanding of which tables should be combined to answer the query.

title: DBRAG: Multi-Table Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Complex Database Queries
text: Adding the row context is crucial in DBRAG, as it enhances the system’s understanding of which tables should be combined to answer the query. Accordingly, for each table ti∈C q, we query the Row Index to retrieve the rows most relevant to the query q. Rows are ranked within each candidate table by the cosine similarity between q and er. The selected rows replace the random rows in the summary, retaining the table name and schema, to form thefine-grained table summary: s+ i ={t Name i , t Schema i , t RelevantRows i }, where tRelevantRows i denotes the set of L relevant rows retrieved from the index. Note:Although the Row Index can be queried directly to obtain a coarse-grained ranking, we use the Table Index to first narrow the candidate set. This design also allows alternative row context selections, such asRandom Rows, to be compared within the same retrieval framework (Section 4.1).

title: DBRAG: Multi-Table Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Complex Database Queries
text: This design also allows alternative row context selections, such asRandom Rows, to be compared within the same retrieval framework (Section 4.1). LLM-based Fine-grained Reranking.Next, we employ a language model L to perform finegrained reranking of the candidate setCq. This step is crucial for addressing (R1), as encoder-based coarse-grained ranking scores each table independently against the query. This focus on individual relevance can limit the selection of tables providing complementary information necessary for answering the query through joins and unions. The LLMbased reranker leverages its reasoning capabilities to consider relationships among the candidate tables, enabling the identification of relevant tables.

This reduced subset of tables, which is semantically relevant to the query and potentially complementary in providing the answer, is passed to the reasoning stage, which we explore next. 3.4 Multi-table Reasoning. To support queries that may require combining data from a varying number of tables while limiting context size (R2), we design a new multi-table reasoner. This component dynamically identifies the subset of tables needed from the retrieved set and generates an execution plan using an LLM integrated with execution tools to run code over the retrieved tables. text: We evaluate our method and baselines focusing on two key tasks: multi-table retrieval and multi-table reasoning. Datasets.Existing tabular QA benchmarks have largely focused on either limited-domain scenarios or single-table contexts. To address this gap, MTQA (Pal et al., 2023) introduced a multi-table QA dataset derived from the cross-domain Spider dataset (Yu et al., 2018), which spans tables from 138 distinct domains. Their work adapts the original text-to-SQL pairs by executing the SQL queries to obtain tabular answers and excluding examples with errors or empty results. In our experiments, we also use the MTQA versions of GeoQuery (GeoQ; Zelle and Mooney, 1996) and ATIS (Price, 1990; Dahl et al., 1994), two smaller multi-table QA datasets built on databases of United States geography and flight booking systems, respectively. Appendix A details the methodology for constructing the database corpora and the queries. It also includes a summary of the key statistics of each dataset.

Specifically, we set the coarsegrained table budget to K= 50 and the finegrained table budget toM= 5 , a design choice that balances precision and recall across diverse user queries. text: Finally, we evaluate the impact of table and row context budgets on both table retrieval and reasoning performance on the Spider dataset. The experiment reveals that while increasing L initially enhances answer accuracy, performance reaches a plateau beyond which additional rows do not consistently improve performance. This aligns with the intuition that only a few rows are needed to grasp the structure and semantics of tabular information.

title: DBRAG: Multi-Table Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Complex Database Queries
text: We propose DBRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework tailored for multi-table question answering. DBRAG overcomes the challenges of complex multi-table relationships by decomposing the task into efficient table retrieval and multi-table reasoning. Our approach leverages a two-stage retrieval strategy, first retrieving candidate tables from the Table Index and then reranking them using query-relevant row context, followed by multi-table chain-of-thought prompting and program-aided execution for precise reasoning. Extensive experiments on multi-table QA datasets demonstrate improvements in both table retrieval and end-to-end QA performance. Our results validate DBRAG as an effective solution for complex, multi-table database question answering. Future work will explore further optimizations and extend support for heterogeneous data integration such as semistructured data and knowledge graphs. 8

text: Building and maintaining the Row Index can be computationally expensive for databases with billions of records. More efficient index construction and maintenance strategies, including sampling approaches potentially drawing on the frequencybased cell selection used by Chen et al. (2024b), could help address these challenges. We leave these issues, along with dynamic schema updates and production deployment, for future work. While the queries in the datasets involve multiple tables, their answers can be obtained by executing SQL queries. In real-world scenarios, however, users may pose more complex queries, such as queries for open-ended exploration or interpretation of trends in the data, which may require analytical reasoning beyond SQL-based operations (Ma et al., 2023). The capability of DBRAG to handle such advanced queries remains unexplored in this paper. Additionally, real-world large databases often present challenges such as noisy data, inconsistencies, and missing information (Hai et al., 2023).

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and AI agents are increasingly embedded in operational business processes. Yet Business Process Management (BPM) curricula and frameworks still largely treat artificial intelligence (AI) as an add-on technology, leaving graduates (as potential future process developers) unprepared to reason about AI as a first-class design element of end-to-end processes. This paper addresses that gap by proposing \emph{AI-decision checkpoints}: explicit moments in a process development trajectory where process developers identify AI-candidate sub-processes, assess expected effects on time, cost, quality, and flexibility, consider legal and organisational constraints, and document a reasoned decision to adopt, constrain, or reject specific AI components. The checkpoints are instantiated through a fictitious customer onboarding process as a \textit{BPM Teaching Case}, embedded in a lifecycle-driven framework spanning six modules that combine process modeling, simulation, workflow execution with AI agents, and process mining, with each module's output serving as the next module's input. A preliminary formative reflection draws on instructor observations, submitted artifacts, and discovered process maps from learning-management-system logs. These exploratory observations suggest that the approach supported clearer distinctions between task-level automation and process-level value.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: Business Process Management (BPM) is a mature information-systems discipline that provides concepts, notations, and methods for identifying, modeling, analyzing, redesigning, executing, and monitoring organizational processes [1, 2]. Core pedagogical content has remained remarkably stable for decades: process discovery and modeling, control-flow analysis, simulation-based performance analysis, workflow enactment, and process mining [3]. This stability is now challenged by advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and AI agents. It has become arXiv:2610.06207v1 [cs.AI] 5 Oct 2026 2 Amin Jalali. technically feasible to introduce AI agents as process participants in knowledgeintensive tasks [4], such as extracting data from unstructured documents, conducting Know-Your-Customer (KYC) or fraud checks, generating customer communication, and lead generation for claim investigation [5]. Industry adoption of such components currently outpaces their curricular integration, leaving graduates at risk of two complementary deficits. Classically trained BPM analysts can model and analyze processes, but struggle to reason about when and how AI components add value at the process level.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: Classically trained BPM analysts can model and analyze processes, but struggle to reason about when and how AI components add value at the process level. Conversely, AI engineers may be able to build proof-of-concept agents and deploy them in production but lack the methodological grounding to assess their impact on end-to-end performance and value creation. Existing curricular responses tend to follow one of two patterns: appending a stand-alone module on AI or LLMs to an otherwise unchanged course, or adding AI-related examples throughout traditional content without altering its structure. In both cases, AI is treated as a technology topic rather than as a design concern to be evaluated systematically across the BPM lifecycle. We contend that the discipline already possesses a suitable backbone for structuring AI-related reasoning: the BPM lifecycle [1], which has long served as a textbook spine and didactic organizer.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: The proposed framework uses the BPM lifecycle to structure a sequence of explicit, phase-related decisions about AI adoption. At each checkpoint, students contribute to determining how AI can enhance processes by identifying AI-candidate subprocesses, establishing the baseline, evaluating expected benefits and risks using the analytical instruments of the corresponding lifecycle phase, and documenting a reasoned decision to adopt, adapt, postpone, or reject specific AI components. This approach decomposes AI adoption from a monolithic yes/no judgment into a chain of locally grounded assessments that distribute AI-related reasoning across all phases, anchor decisions in established BPM instruments, and produce a traceable decision trail that can be revisited. The framework does not prescribe a correct answer at any checkpoint; it foregrounds reasoning quality, requiring students to articulate assumptions, acknowledge trade-offs, and justify decisions. One checkpoint aligns with each lifecycle phase: identification, discovery, analysis, redesign, implementation, and monitoring [1]; individual checkpoints can be weighted or combined without disrupting the logic. section: 3.1 CP1 - Process Identification: Scoping AI Opportunities
text: Each candidate’s expected impact is assessed along thedevil’s quadrangle(time, cost, quality, flexibility) [10], and risks are cataloged covering legal and regulatory requirements (e.g. GDPR), ethical considerations, data availability, and organizational readiness. The outcome is an AI opportunity register that combines benefit assessments with initial technical feasibility in a prioritization matrix, determining which candidates proceed to later phases.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
section: 3.2 CP2 - Process Discovery: Positioning AI in the As-Is Process
text: CP2 is located in the process-discovery phase. The focus shifts from the process landscape to a concrete as-is process, and from abstract opportunity identification to a precise understanding of how candidates from CP1 relate to existing organizational work. The guiding question is:given a description of the selected 6 Amin Jalali. process, where would the AI candidates conceptually attach, and which human and system actors would they interact with or affect? The as-is process in this phase shall be specified as a normative model and enriched with an explicit actor perspective. Candidates prioritized in CP1 are positioned with respect to this model rather than integrated into it. For each candidate, the analysis specifies (i) the segment of the as-is model it would conceptually replace, support, or augment, (ii) the human roles and IT systems currently involved at that segment and how they would be affected, and (iii) the inputs, outputs, and control transfers currently observed.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
section: 3.2 CP2 - Process Discovery: Positioning AI in the As-Is Process
text: For each candidate, the analysis specifies (i) the segment of the as-is model it would conceptually replace, support, or augment, (ii) the human roles and IT systems currently involved at that segment and how they would be affected, and (iii) the inputs, outputs, and control transfers currently observed. Escalation paths, approval steps, and exception-handling mechanisms that would become relevant under AI augmentation are also sketched at a conceptual level. The artifact is the as-is process model together with an AI-positioning note that records, for each candidate, its intended placement, the actors affected, and prominent structural obstacles or dependencies.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: CP3 is located in the process-analysis phase. While CP1 and CP2 establish where AI augmentation is promising and how it relates to the as-is process, CP3 quantifies the current performance without altering the process structure. The guiding question is:given an executable representation of the current process, what is the baseline performance against which any redesign (AI-based or otherwise) must be assessed? The baseline can be identified in different ways such as extracting the current state of the process using process mining, or transforming the model from CP2 into an executable model and simulating the process to identify the baseline. In courses without prior process data, the latter approach can be feasible; while in practical settings, other approaches can be followed. Regardless of the method, the analysis should yield baseline indicators such as average throughput times, waiting times, resource utilization, and sensitivity to workload variation.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: Regardless of the method, the analysis should yield baseline indicators such as average throughput times, waiting times, resource utilization, and sensitivity to workload variation. The artifact produced at CP3 is a baseline performance report documenting the chosen method, underlying assumptions, and key performance indicators, with particular attention to structural bottlenecks and systematic delays. The importance is to define a baseline against which upcoming changes can be evaluated (whether AI-driven or otherwise). Crucially, where a simulation model is established as part of this baseline, it serves as a reusable analytical asset: as redesign proposals emerge in later phases, the model can be refined to reflect the proposed changes and re-simulated to assess their expected impact before any real implementation takes place.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
section: 3.4 CP4 - Process Redesign: Value-Aware Business Process Redesign
text: CP4 is located in the process-redesign phase. Building on the baseline from CP3 and the conceptual positioning from CP1 and CP2, it treats AI augmentation as one design option within a broader redesign effort. The guiding question is: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 7 when redesign practices are applied, under which conditions does the inclusion of AI-candidate subprocesses produce to-be process models that outperform the baseline? Starting from the executable as-is model and diagnosed weaknesses, the redesign uses recognized principles (task elimination, resequencing, parallelization, integration of responsibilities). To-be scenarios include both classical control-flow and resource changes and variants that embed AI candidates, integrating AI with redesign moves rather than bolting it on.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
section: 3.4 CP4 - Process Redesign: Value-Aware Business Process Redesign
text: To-be scenarios include both classical control-flow and resource changes and variants that embed AI candidates, integrating AI with redesign moves rather than bolting it on. Redesign variants are distinguished by the AI technology embedded: (i) LLM-based agents for email intake and structured data extraction from documents, (ii) RAG-equipped agents for fraud screening that retrieve and reason over AML rule documents, and (iii) classical BPM redesign variants without AI components, which serve as the comparison baseline. All scenarios are simulated under consistent assumptions and compared to the baseline. The artifact is a comparative redesign-and-simulation dossier in which each candidate is assigned a redesign decision, justified by the redesign rationale and quantitative evidence, including trade-offs such as bottleneck relocation or increased process complexity.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
section: 3.5 CP5 - Process Implementation: Realisability and Governance
text: CP5 is located in the implementation phase and addresses the gap between conceptual redesign and technical realization. The guiding question is:are the AIaugmented redesign decisions technically realizable within the selected workflow and AI infrastructure? The to-be design is mapped onto a concrete workflow platform and integrated with specific AI services, such as LLM APIs or RAG pipelines. For each AI component, required data flows, performance characteristics, error-handling mechanisms, and security and privacy constraints are matched against what the infrastructure can provide. Where the platform does not natively support the required control-flow patterns or error-handling logic, compensating structures are introduced, for instance, additional validation activities, schema-constrained prompts, explicit human approval tasks, or fallback paths triggered on AI failure or low confidence. The artifact is an implementation feasibility and governance dossier per AI component. The artifact is an implementation feasibility and governance dossier per AI component. It records the extent to which the component could be realized as designed, the workarounds introduced, the governance measures put in place (logging, thresholds, escalation rules, human-in-the-loop points), and any residual technical or organizational risks.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: CP6 is located in the monitoring-and-controlling phase and concerns the expost evaluation of AI-augmented subprocesses on the basis of execution data. The guiding question is:given execution data of the deployed process, do the 8 Amin Jalali. AI-augmented subprocesses behave as intended and deliver net value over time, or should the process be redesigned and reconfigured? Execution data are collected as event logs once the deployed process has run sufficiently; in a course setting, pre-generated logs are typically provided. Process discovery is applied and tested against the normative to-be model from CP4/CP5; conformance analysis surfaces deviations such as bypassed AI-enabled subprocesses; and performance analysis quantifies indicators against the CP3 baseline and CP4 simulated expectations. The artifact is a mining-based evaluation summary consolidating execution patterns, conformance deviations, and realized performance. Its insights feed back into CP1, completing the evidencebased governance cycle.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: The framework was instantiated in a Master ’s-level course for students in the final year of a Business Information Systems or Computer Science program. The course has been coordinated by the author for more than 15 years and is designed based on experience-based learning [11]. No prior knowledge of BPM or AI was assumed. A total of 152 students enrolled in the course. Of these, 29 had passed the group assignments in a previous year and were required to participate only in the individual exam; the remaining 123 were new students who formed 25 project groups, each with a maximum of five members. The course mandates group work, with results delivered at each module milestone. A key structural principle is theevolving-artifactorganization: each module’s output becomes the next module’s input, so students revisit AI-related decisions repeatedly with accumulating evidence.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: The primary deliverable of this paper is the Banking case. The six modules (M1- M6) are built around this case, where students focus on designing a customer onboarding process comprising customer registration, fraud assessment, and approval, at a fictitious retail bank facing a scalability crisis. The case is intentionally rich in regulatory constraints, knowledge-intensive work, and heterogeneous data sources, which together make it suitable for realistic AI augmentation scenarios. It is structured around two main documents alongside other instructions distributed to students at different points in the course. Document A(released at M1, needed for M2) describes the current as-is process. Seven roles are involved: a clerk who registers scanned customer requests, a credit investigator who checks customer credits via an external service, two CRM officers who manage customer communications and profile activation, an accounting assistant who enables transactions, and two fraud investigators who manually review each case against the bank’s anti-money-laundering (AML) guidebooks.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: Seven roles are involved: a clerk who registers scanned customer requests, a credit investigator who checks customer credits via an external service, two CRM officers who manage customer communications and profile activation, an accounting assistant who enables transactions, and two fraud investigators who manually review each case against the bank’s anti-money-laundering (AML) guidebooks. The normal scenario traces a case from registration through credit AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 9 check, parallel profile and account activation, customer notification, fraud review, and either full access or external fraud investigation. A cancellation scenario (needed and can be released at M4) introduces a regulatory constraint on when a customer can withdraw the case, which is before an external fraud investigation returns a positive result, requiring a carefully bounded cancel region.

text: A cancellation scenario (needed and can be released at M4) introduces a regulatory constraint on when a customer can withdraw the case, which is before an external fraud investigation returns a positive result, requiring a carefully bounded cancel region. Document B(released at M3) describes the redesign brief: the bank cannot scale with the current manual process and proposes a combination of AI agents, where students are guided to prioritize email-based registration extraction and RAG-based fraud screening, as well as web-service automation (credit checks, profile and transaction management, police reporting). The fraudscreening agent is deliberately constrained by a known class-imbalance problem (the data science team reports high recall but imperfect precision), so students must reason about when the agent’s output can be trusted autonomously and when a human must remain in the loop.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: The fraudscreening agent is deliberately constrained by a known class-imbalance problem (the data science team reports high recall but imperfect precision), so students must reason about when the agent’s output can be trusted autonomously and when a human must remain in the loop. The hook of the case is established in M1: students build a working prototype of the email-intake AI agent before they have modeled the process, then are asked whether deploying it would actually help the bank. The tension between “the agent works” and “we don’t yet know if it adds value” motivates the entire lifecycle journey that follows. Case materials, module instructions, and datasets are openly available in a GitHub repository 1.

Teaching notes, discussion guidance, and sample solutions are available to instructors upon request. 4.2 Module 1 - Process Identification, BPM and AI Foundations, and CP1 The first module (M1) introduces the conceptual foundations required to apply the framework: a concise overview of BPM and its evolution, the BPM lifecycle, and core notions such as processes, subprocesses, and actors, together with an introduction to the AI technologies most relevant to BPM: Large Language Models (LLMs), generative AI, and AI agents. On this basis, the banking case is presented, and students construct a process architecture for the bank. Within this architecture, they identify AI-candidate subprocesses, documenting their assumptions as artifacts introduced in CP1.

section: 4.5 Module 4 - BPMN-Centric Process Redesign and CP4
text: M4 refines the best M3 scenario in BPMN (usingSignavioandTrisotech), shifting from happy-path to exception-handling redesign. Students apply established modeling guidelines to clarify control flow, make subprocess boundaries explicit, and model human-system-AI interactions and cancellation scenarios. This enables a second pass on CP4, revisiting AI-augmented subprocess choices in light of representational clarity and implementability. The artifact is a consolidated BPMN-based redesign model with clearly identified AI-augmented subprocesses and associated redesign principles. Together with the analytical evidence from M3, this model constitutes the final outcome of CP4 and provides the basis for the feasibility and governance analysis in M5.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
section: 4.6 Module 5 - Implementation in Workflow Platforms and CP5
text: The fifth module (M5) addresses the implementation phase and operationalizes CP5. Building on the selected and refined BPMN-based to-be model from M4, students map the preferred redesign onto a concrete AI-augmented workflow in n8n. The emphasis is on realizing the control-flow structures and subprocess boundaries defined in BPMN and on technically integrating the AI-augmented subprocesses retained after CP4. AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 11 Students decompose the BPMN model into an executable workflow and realize AI-augmented subprocesses as concrete agents: an email-intake agent for document extraction and a RAG-based fraud-assessment agent that retrieves and reasons over AML rules embedded inQdrant, with a human-in-the-loop step for flagged cases. The fraud agent introduces students to configuring semantic memory within a workflow platform. CP5 is discharged by assessing, for each AI-augmented subprocess, the extent to which the BPMN-level design from M4 can be realized and governed in the chosen technical environment.

text: CP5 is discharged by assessing, for each AI-augmented subprocess, the extent to which the BPMN-level design from M4 can be realized and governed in the chosen technical environment. The resulting dossier documents (i) alignment between design and implementation, (ii) workarounds and additional control structures introduced (validation and enrichment steps, schema-constrained prompts, fallback paths on AI failure), and (iii) governance and oversight mechanisms. On this basis, the redesign-level decisions from CP4 are refined into implementation decisions.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: At the time of writing, the exam has not yet been administered, so the evaluation focuses on group performance in labs and assignments. Given the single-course, single-instructor design with no comparison group and no final exam data at the time of writing, all findings below should be read as a preliminary, exploratory reflection on experience rather than as evidence of learning effectiveness. The evaluation addresses three questions: (EQ1) Do students engage with AI adoption as expected phase-specific decision? (EQ2) How is submission timing distributed across modules, and what does this imply for course design? (EQ3) How do students perceive the learning value of each module’s primary activity? Evidence triangulates instructor observations with insights discovered from LMS event logs extracted by PM4Moodle [14], a voluntary end-of-course group survey (conducted per groups), which capture group interactions at checkpoints. Given the single-instantiation design, findings are presented as preliminary indications rather than generalizable results.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: To illustrate how checkpoints encouraged students to evaluate AI adoption during process development, we describe a pattern observed in the CP4 artifacts. Most groups identified the email-intake and fraud-assessment subprocesses as AI candidates in CP1 after receiving feedback, and the majority initially expected substantial reductions in throughput time; in several cases, they estimated that AI-based intake would halve overall case cycle time. After completing the baseline simulation in CP3, these groups found that the bottleneck lay not in registration but in the two-person fraud-investigation queue, which operated near full utilization. Their CP4 comparative redesign dossiers explicitly recorded revised AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 13 assessments: the email-intake agent, while technically functional, was projected to shift the bottleneck downstream rather than reduce end-to-end cycle time unless the fraud-investigation subprocess was redesigned with the help of a second AI agent equipped with RAG.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: Their CP4 comparative redesign dossiers explicitly recorded revised AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 13 assessments: the email-intake agent, while technically functional, was projected to shift the bottleneck downstream rather than reduce end-to-end cycle time unless the fraud-investigation subprocess was redesigned with the help of a second AI agent equipped with RAG. These groups consequently reclassified the intake agent from a high-priority candidate to a medium-priority one, conditional on redesigning the fraud investigation with the help of an AI agent and applying a re-sequence pattern to do it earlier in the process. This pattern of initial overestimation followed by evidence-driven revision was evident in the written justifications attached to CP4 artifacts and was confirmed through instructor observations during group supervision sessions. It illustrates the intended function of the checkpoint chain: not to discourage AI adoption, but to ground it in process-level evidence accumulated across phases.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: This paper presented the Banking case and the AI-decision checkpoint framework that structures it. Six checkpoints, one per BPM lifecycle phase, turn the lifecycle from a passive organizer into a chain of evidence-grounded decisions about AI adoption, instantiated in a Master-level course with a continuously evolving banking onboarding artifact. Formative evidence suggests three preliminary conclusions. First, checkpoints appeared to encourage students to treat AI as conditional on process-level value: groups revised initial over-estimates once simulation evidence accumulated, and incorporated governance structures in their BPMN and implementation artifacts. Second, the discovered process map from LMS’s log characterizes submissiontiming patterns and highlights two actionable adjustments: deferring cancellation patterns to M4 and adding a CP1 submission touchpoint for systematic data capture.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
text: Second, the discovered process map from LMS’s log characterizes submissiontiming patterns and highlights two actionable adjustments: deferring cancellation patterns to M4 and adding a CP1 submission touchpoint for systematic data capture. Third, a voluntary group survey (10 of 24 groups) indicates that students perceived positive learning value across all modules (all medians≥4), with M5 implementation activities receiving the highest ratings, consistent with the LMS evidence that prior checkpoints appeared to have effectively scaffolded that phase. For educators, the framework integrates AI into existing BPM courses without replacing the lifecycle backbone or mandating specific tools. The key transferable principle is theevolving-artifactstructure, which ensures students revisit AI decisions with accumulating evidence rather than treating each module as an independent exercise. Future work will extend LMS instrumentation for richer data capture per checkpoint and, after several course runs, codify recurrent reasoning patterns into structured checkpoint templates to support adoption in other institutional contexts.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: Continuous ingestion can expose new retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) content to retrieval before vetting completes, creating a temporal attack surface that conventional admission decisions do not capture. We present a fail-closed provisional-visibility protocol that admits new content under a deadline, hides items whose verification has not committed in time, and supports lineage-scoped containment. The protocol bounds unvetted exposure by the configured visibility budget plus query-path enforcement delay; poisoning exposure remains conditional on verifier correctness. We evaluate the design on five workloads of encoded natural-language documents using an exact backend and Milvus. Under verifier backlog, the deadline reduced median poisoned retrievals from 34 (29--34) to 7 (6--7) relative to asynchronous admission without a deadline, with the same reduction in displaced clean results. Verify-before-visible avoided provisional exposure but delayed clean first visibility to 6.3 s, whereas provisional admission made content visible within 3 ms; expired clean items could nevertheless experience temporary availability gaps. Replaying decisions from a recipe-specific detector illustrated the protocol boundary: false promotions left poison visible, while false refusals excluded clean content from retrieval. Standalone Milvus tests characterized enforcement delay and concurrent HNSW retrieval on one node. These results clarify which guarantees come from the protocol and which outcomes depend on detector quality, while quantifying the freshness and availability trade-offs.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG V ector Stores Chuhong Xu Sony Corporate of America San Jose, USA chuhong.xu@sony.com Lu Yi Google LLC Mountain View, USA annabelyi@google.com Gangzhen Qian Google LLC Mountain View, USA irisqian@google.com Kainan Zhou Google LLC Mountain View, USA zhoumark@google.com Zhaoyi Li Independent Researcher Mountain View, USA lzy9776@gmail.com Hang Xiao F ortinet, Inc. Sunnyvale, USA xhang@fortinet.com Abstract—Continuous ingestion can expose new retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) content to retrieval before vetting completes, creating a temporal attack surface that conventional admission decisions do not capture. We present a fail-closed provisional-visibility protocol that admits new content under a deadline, hides items whose veriﬁcation has not committed in time, and supports lineage-scoped containment. The protocol bounds unvetted exposure by the conﬁgured visibility budget plus query-path enforcement delay; poisoning exposure remains conditional on veriﬁer correctness. We evaluate the design on ﬁve workloads of encoded natural-language documents using an exact backend and Milvus.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: We evaluate the design on ﬁve workloads of encoded natural-language documents using an exact backend and Milvus. Under veriﬁer backlog, the deadline reduced median poisoned retrievals from 34 (29–34) to 7 (6–7) relative to asynchronous admission without a deadline, with the same reduction in displaced clean results. V erify-before-visible avoided provisional exposure but delayed clean ﬁrst visibility to 6.3 s, whereas provisional admission made content visible within 3 ms; expired clean items could nevertheless experience temporary availability gaps. Replaying decisions from a recipe-speciﬁc detector illustrated the protocol boundary: false promotions left poison visible, while false refusals excluded clean content from retrieval. Standalone Milvus tests characterized enforcement delay and concurrent HNSW retrieval on one node. These results clarify which guarantees come from the protocol and which outcomes depend on detector quality, while quantifying the freshness and availability trade-offs. Index Terms —stream ingestion, admission control, systems security, retrieval-augmented generation, vector databases, data poisoning I.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: Index Terms —stream ingestion, admission control, systems security, retrieval-augmented generation, vector databases, data poisoning I. I NTRODUCTION Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds a language model’s output on documents retrieved from an external knowledge base [1], and dense passage retrieval turns that lookup into embedding-similarity search, commonly served by a vector store [2]. As deployments move from static corpora to live knowledge, that store must absorb new content while serving queries. Streaming RAG refreshes the knowledge base as content arrives [3], while versioned vector lakes retain temporal views over continuous updates [4]. Both aim to reduce freshness delay. Low freshness delay and trust assessment are in tension: establishing that a newly arrived item is trustworthy takes time because it requires checking provenance, scanning for adversarial or promotional manipulation, and comparing against existing knowledge. A freshness objective instead pushes the same item toward the query path as soon as possible.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: A freshness objective instead pushes the same item toward the query path as soon as possible. Systems with aggressive freshness objectives may therefore permit provisional content to become query-visible before veriﬁcation completes. This is a design option, not a requirement: keeping unveriﬁed content invisible until fully vetted avoids unvetted exposure at the cost of veriﬁcationdependent freshness delay, a policy we retain as a baseline. We study the security consequences of the low-latency operating point and how to constrain them. Admitting content before it is vetted creates an exposure interval. Corpus-poisoning attacks can steer dense retrievers with a small injected set, including for unseen queries [5], and PoisonedRAG further shows that a few injected texts can induce attacker-chosen answers in an end-to-end RAG pipeline [6]. In a continuously ingested store, that exposure is fundamentally temporal: a provisionally admitted poisoned vector can be retrieved throughout the window between ﬁrst visibility and containment, whether or not a detector eventually ﬂags it.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: In a continuously ingested store, that exposure is fundamentally temporal: a provisionally admitted poisoned vector can be retrieved throughout the window between ﬁrst visibility and containment, whether or not a detector eventually ﬂags it. This temporal systems view falls between existing lines: poisoning defenses report detection effectiveness on static or batch-constructed knowledge bases, and continuously updated vector stores are mature but security-agnostic (Sec. VIII). We present a fail-closed provisional-visibility protocol for streaming vector stores. New content is query-visible but bounded by a conﬁgurable visibility deadline Tp; only positive multi-signal veriﬁcation promotes an item; expiry hides it instead. A deadline scheduler decoupled from the veriﬁcation queue makes that guarantee survive veriﬁer backlog, and content later found malicious is excluded from retrieval by lineage-scoped containment without rebuilding the store. This paper makes four contributions. C1 (Formalization). We deﬁne unvetted exposure Eu, poisoning exposure Ep, containment, and recovery as distinct intervals, separating what a protocol can guarantee ( Eu) from what depends on detector quality ( Ep). C2 (Protocol). We design a fail-closed provisional-visibility protocol whose invariants I1–I7 guarantee that unveriﬁed content cannot remain query-visible beyond Tp + δhide and that each item is provisionally visible at most once. A metadata time-to-live alone does not give this: an expiry that queues behind the veriﬁer inherits its backlog. C3 (Containment).

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: C3 (Containment). We implement lineage-scoped containment that excludes a compromised item’s descendants from the query path before physical purging completes, and measure its collateral revocation. C4 (Evaluation). We quantify deadline effectiveness and clean-content cost, evaluate a recipespeciﬁc feasibility detector and replay its decisions through the promotion path, characterize eligibility completeness, and evaluate δhide and hierarchical navigable small world (HNSW) behavior on standalone Milvus. II. B ACKGROUND AND THREAT MODEL A RAG pipeline embeds a query, retrieves the top- k nearest chunks from a vector store and conditions generation on them; under continuous ingestion an upstream stream is chunked, embedded and inserted while queries are served. We model the store as an insert path and a query path that observe a per-item visibility state. A. Threat model We assume an adversary who can submit content into the ingestion stream or control an already-authorized source. The adversary may optimize against the retriever and any known lightweight admission signal.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: The adversary may optimize against the retriever and any known lightweight admission signal. Prior work shows high attack success from a few retrieval-targeted texts [6]; SilentRetrieval further demonstrates a ﬂuency-constrained evasive variant [7]. Injection is at a bounded rate (0.1–5% of the stream), steady or bursty, with retrieval results observable. A poisoned item succeeds if it is retrieved for a target query before it is contained. The adversary cannot modify admission metadata, the deadline scheduler, per-item visibility state, or provenance records; fully compromised veriﬁers, a malicious control-plane operator, and embedding-model backdoors are out of scope. We do admit trusted-source compromise: an item may carry valid provenance yet be malicious. In RAGShield’s numericalclaim setting, an insider with valid signing credentials reduces provenance-only admission to the no-defense attack-success rate [8]. We therefore do not rely on provenance alone for promotion (Sec. IV -C). B.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: B. Scope We defend the ingestion-to-retrieval lifecycle of a single vector-store deployment as observed through its supported query path; the detector/veriﬁer is a pluggable component throughout. Strict multi-replica/cache consistency and fully distributed rollback are out of scope (Sec. IX). III. P ROBLEM FORMALIZATION For an ingested item x we distinguish the lifecycle timestamps tarrive, tvisible (ﬁrst retrievable through the supported query path), tdetect, tcontain (no longer returned by the query path), tpurge (physically deleted from the live store) and taudit. The visibility deadline is anchored to ﬁrst visibility, tdeadline = tvisible + Tp; anchoring to arrival instead shifts Eu by the small admission-to-visibility gap. Freshness delay is D f = tvisible − tarrive and recovery is Wrecovery = tpurge − tdetect; physical live-store purge is treated separately from logical containment.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: Freshness delay is D f = tvisible − tarrive and recovery is Wrecovery = tpurge − tdetect; physical live-store purge is treated separately from logical containment. We deﬁne unvetted exposure as the interval during which unveriﬁed content is query-visible, with both endpoints on the query path: Eu(x) = tqp-exit(x) − tvisible(x), where tqp-exit is when the path stops returning x as unvetted, after promotion, rejection or expiry. We deﬁne poisoning exposure as the interval during which a malicious item can inﬂuence retrieval, Ep(x) = tcontain(x) − tﬁrst-poison-visible(x); it depends on detector false negatives and promotion policy, so the protocol bounds it only when the veriﬁer never falsely promotes. We deﬁne enforcement delay to record that a metadata state change is not containment until the query path honors it: with texpire the deadline instant and tqp-hide the moment the query path stops returning x, δhide(x) = tqp-hide(x) − texpire(x). The guarantee has three layers. (i) Operational bound.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: (i) Operational bound. Expiry ﬁres at tvisible + Tp whatever the veriﬁer is doing, because the scheduler does not share its queue, and the query path stops returning the item δhide later: Eu(x) ≤ Tp(x) +δhide(x). (1) Only query-path visibility counts, so exposure ends at tqp-hide rather than at the earlier control-plane transition; anchoring there would put δhide outside the interval and make (1) true by arithmetic. Equation (1) separates the conﬁgured deadline from a deployment-speciﬁc enforcement slack. The latter comprises scheduler ﬁring, state commit, and query-path propagation (Sec. VI-A); each is ﬁnite only while the control plane is live, so operators must provision and monitor δhide. The protocol makes that term independent of veriﬁer backlog: a separate scheduler and an O(1) ﬂag write provide it, although shared-resource contention can still affect its magnitude. (ii) Conditional poison bound. For a malicious item never falsely promoted, the same bound applies to Ep. (iii) General case.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: (iii) General case. After false promotion, exposure is governed by detector error and later containment. We therefore retain an oracle arm as a mechanism upper bound and separately evaluate one recipespeciﬁc detector and its lifecycle consequences (Sec. VII). IV. S YSTEM DESIGN A. Architecture An admission control plane assigns new content a risk score r(x) and visibility budget Tp(x), then inserts it as PROVI- SIONAL. V eriﬁer workers and the deadline scheduler consume INGESTED not visible PROVISIONAL visible TRUSTED visible REVOKED terminal QUARANTINED not visible HIDDEN not visible admit verify pass by Tp revoke hard fail fail deadline late pass late fail Fig. 1. Protocol state machine. Shaded states are query-visible. Deadline expiry only hides; a late pass enters TRUSTED directly, so each item has at most one provisional episode. that state independently. The query path reads an authoritative ﬂag, admits PROVISIONAL and TRUSTED items to the same top-k competition without trust-based reranking, and excludes all other states.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: The query path reads an authoritative ﬂag, admits PROVISIONAL and TRUSTED items to the same top-k competition without trust-based reranking, and excludes all other states. Physical deletion remains off the critical path. B. Item state machine Fig. 1 gives the atomic compare-and-set transitions; competing veriﬁcation and deadline events are ordered by commit time (Sec. IV -D). C. Positive veriﬁcation and hard gates Promotion requires afﬁrmative decisions from noncompensating source/integrity ( S) and content/behavior ( C) families; C is mandatory under trusted-source compromise. D1 instantiates this contract. The S family checks credential validity, provenance consistency and the pinned encoder revision. The C family sums calibration-standardized half-passage cosine repetition and distance to the ten nearest corpus posts after excluding the item’s source group. Its threshold 1.3553 maximized poison-class F1 on 448 calibration groups, then remained ﬁxed for a single evaluation on 512 disjoint test groups; D1 received neither test labels nor evaluation queries.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: Its threshold 1.3553 maximized poison-class F1 on 448 calibration groups, then remained ﬁxed for a single evaluation on 512 disjoint test groups; D1 received neither test labels nor evaluation queries. Only the content family contributes detector-quality evidence; the source-family controls validate interface plumbing. D. Deadline enforcement and atomic transitions Fail-closed enforcement rests on decoupling. A dedicated scheduler, driven by per-item deadlines and independent of the veriﬁer queue, performs expiration; hiding is an O(1) visibility-state transition honored by the query path through the authoritative ﬂag, waiting neither for veriﬁcation nor for physical deletion. The enforcement delay δhide therefore does not queue behind the veriﬁer, the property on which (1) rests under load.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: The enforcement delay δhide therefore does not queue behind the veriﬁer, the property on which (1) rests under load. Because a deadline and a veriﬁcation result may occur concurrently, all transitions are atomic compare-and-set operations conditioned on the current state, and the race is resolved by commit time: a promotion succeeds only if the item is still PROVISIONAL and the positive veriﬁcation committed no later than the deadline; otherwise the scheduler commits PROVISIONAL → HIDDEN and a late positive result commits HIDDEN → TRUSTED idempotently. A veriﬁcation that ﬁnishes computing before the deadline but commits after it is thus post-deadline, so a veriﬁer cannot use its internal completion time to extend visibility. E. Lineage-scoped containment and recovery Each vector carries lineage metadata: document ID, source and version, ingestion batch, embedding-model version, chunk parent, and vector ID.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: Lineage-scoped containment and recovery Each vector carries lineage metadata: document ID, source and version, ingestion batch, embedding-model version, chunk parent, and vector ID. A trusted item is revoked following a later veriﬁer alert or a source/lineage revocation event, such as a credential judged compromised or a batch ﬂagged by an operator. Continuous per-item large language model (LLM) monitoring is out of scope. Containment revokes only the affected lineage rather than rebuilding the store. Operationally, operators should choose the narrowest scope the alert evidence justiﬁes: source scope for a compromised publisher or credential, batch or version scope for a suspect ingestion unit, and item scope only when the affected object is localized and lineage is reliable. A scope narrower than the evidence may leave correlated descendants visible, while a broader one increases clean collateral removal.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: A scope narrower than the evidence may leave correlated descendants visible, while a broader one increases clean collateral removal. Logical containment, an O(1) exclusion, occurs when the supported query path no longer returns the item and ends measured poisoning exposure ( tcontain); physical live-store purge is deﬁned separately through recovery latency ( Wrecovery), so a security metric is not conﬂated with database garbage collection. The query-path guarantee establishes exclusion rather than erasure. Operationally, before live-store purge completes, a hidden vector may still occupy index storage; snapshots or exports can preserve it afterward. Revocation tombstones must therefore be retained and honored during restore and rebuild for as long as such copies exist. Access control and audit remain necessary until all retained copies are deleted. F . Protocol invariants Each invariant maps to a tested property. I1–I2 require afﬁrmative S and C decisions with no hard-gate failure; the oracle tests the promotion outcome and D1 the concrete decision path.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: I1–I2 require afﬁrmative S and C decisions with no hard-gate failure; the oracle tests the promotion outcome and D1 the concrete decision path. I3 makes expiry hide, I4 enforces (1), I5 ends exposure at logical containment, I6 decouples expiry from veriﬁcation and deletion, and I7 permits one provisional episode. Lifecycle invariants I3–I7 run in both arms. A riskdependent Tp(x) = f (r(x)) changes none of them. V. I MPLEMENTATION We implement the control plane on a streaming vectorstore stack. Content arrives through an asynchronous ingestion producer and is routed by an admission service that applies the cheap hard gate and assigns the visibility deadline, then inserts admitted items into a single Milvus [9] collection. PROVISIONAL and TRUSTED are eligibility states in the control store rather than separate collections: promotion ﬂips state and moves no vector, and the query service serves both under one top- k (Sec. IV -A).

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: IV -A). The authoritative item metadata (visibility state, deadline, lineage, and audit timestamps) lives in a separate lightweight control store, not in the vector database, which holds vectors and serves retrieval while the query service decides eligibility. Manu retains row-level ACID while explicitly relaxing complex transaction requirements for vector workloads [10]. Our protocol needs atomic transitions over those ﬁelds, so they remain in the control store. Under post-ﬁltering, updating the visibility ﬂag is an O(1) write that the query path honors immediately and that is decoupled from deletion or compaction. The timer-ordered scheduler does not share the veriﬁer pool; together, these two forms of decoupling realize I6. Transitions are compare-and-set updates (Sec. IV -D), and lineage columns enable scoped revocation without a rebuild. The veriﬁer interface has two instantiations. A deterministic oracle isolates lifecycle timing; the detector arm replays heldout D1 decisions and measured detector-only service times through the same promotion path.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: A deterministic oracle isolates lifecycle timing; the detector arm replays heldout D1 decisions and measured detector-only service times through the same promotion path. It therefore captures observed errors and latency but excludes online detector and model contention. A single-process in-memory harness validates the control plane without noise. The same interface can be backed by a real vector store. Section VI-C compares the resulting post-retrieval eligibility check with an in-index ﬁlter. The harness, preregistrations and authoritative result ﬁles are available from the authors, each recording the runtime-code ﬁngerprint it was produced under. VI. E VALUATION SETUP We ask whether Eu is bounded and how much the enforcement delay δhide widens it; whether that bound survives veriﬁer overload; how freshness trades against exposure over Tp; what top-k completeness cost eligibility enforcement imposes; and how precise containment is. A separate experiment reports HNSW index ﬁdelity [11] and descriptive single-node throughput and tail latency across ﬁve independently restarted Milvus Standalone processes (Sec. VII-G). A.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: A. Instrumentation and derived metrics Every lifecycle metric derives from one versioned event schema of per-item timestamps, so the standalone deployment emits the same ﬁelds without changing a deﬁnition. Three distinctions matter. (i) tverify-end ̸= tverify-commit: a result committed after the deadline is post-deadline (Sec. IV -D). (ii) Scheduler ﬁring, state commit and query-path propagation are components of δhide, not extra terms in (1); observed through probes, it is interval-censored, so we report the conservative upper bound and never charge the probe interval to system delay. (iii) Per-query item state is logged as observed at return time, never reconstructed from the item’s later state, which is what the residual exposure rate depends on. B. Workloads, baselines, and parameters Four workload classes stress different facets: ingestion under concurrent retrieval, a poison burst, a veriﬁer slowdown exercising I6, and post-promotion revocation.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: Workloads, baselines, and parameters Four workload classes stress different facets: ingestion under concurrent retrieval, a poison burst, a veriﬁer slowdown exercising I6, and post-promotion revocation. Each poisonburst workload is generated from scratch: an eight-topic corpus of 600 unit vectors, eight queries from the attacked topic for crafting and eight more, disjoint, for measurement, eight from other topics as controls, and six poison vectors perturbed toward the crafting queries alone. Queries are issued at a ﬁxed rate over a ﬁxed window with the poison injected partway in, using ﬁve ﬁxed seeds, all retained. Four baselines share one ingestion path and differ only in admission policy: B1 0 .5 1 Tp 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 time since ingestion (s) poisoned top- k rate B1 none B2 pre-vet B3 no deadline B4 ours Fig. 2.

Poisoned top- k rate over time on the crafted query set (Milvus Lite), pooled over ﬁve workloads; one bin is one query rotation, below which the rate is undersampled by construction. B3 holds at the undefended baseline’s rate until veriﬁcation drains, B4 is cut at Tp, and B1 is never contained within the window. Only the backlogged condition is drawn: with the veriﬁer keeping up, B3 and B4 coincide. immediate admission with no veriﬁcation, B2 synchronous verify-before-visible, B3 async visible with no deadline, and B4 the proposed protocol. B3 isolates the deadline’s own effect, differing from B4 in nothing else. The deadline Tp is swept over points bracketing the veriﬁer’s own latency. C.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: C. Eligibility enforcement A post-retrieval authoritative check (post-ﬁlter) and an inindex metadata ﬁlter trade off along three axes: δhide, query latency, and retrieval completeness. Post-ﬁltering gives a small δhide because the control store is authoritative, but it ﬁlters after approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search, so it can under- ﬁll the top- k; the in-index ﬁlter avoids under-ﬁll but its hide observability is left to the store’s read-consistency level [10], which we ﬁx and report. With α over-fetch and pool size M = αk, post-ﬁltering under-ﬁlls exactly when pool hidden occupancy hM(q) exceeds 1 −1/α, so under-ﬁll is governed by the upper tail of hM and not its mean. We therefore vary three hidden distributions: uniform-random, semantic-clustered, and query-coupled. The query-coupled set is built with knowledge of the evaluation queries, so it is a worst case by construction; the eligible population stays ≥ k, so exact ground truth stays well deﬁned.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: The query-coupled set is built with knowledge of the evaluation queries, so it is a worst case by construction; the eligible population stays ≥ k, so exact ground truth stays well deﬁned. Completeness is reported as under-ﬁll (result count < k) and Eligible Recall@ k against exact brute-force ground truth, plus Conditional Recall@ k given a full- k result, which isolates ANN approximation error. D. Invariant validation and reporting Automated tests assert that timeout never promotes, that each item enters PROVISIONAL at most once, that a postdeadline-committed pass ﬁres HIDDEN → TRUSTED rather than PROVISIONAL → TRUSTED, that HIDDEN and RE- VOKED items are never returned, and that logical containment holds while physical purge is pending. An overload test injects heavy veriﬁer backlog and conﬁrms unvetted items still leave the visible set within Tp + δhide. VII.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: VII. R ESULTS The exact and Milvus Lite tiers validate lifecycle mechanics and eligible ground truth; D1 adds measured decisions, and Standalone adds HNSW with 1–16-client load. A. Deadline enforcement under veriﬁcation backlog The harness validates invariants I1–I7 and the commit-time rule (20/20 checks). The real-time functional slice runs the full ingest → provisional → deadline → hide → late-verify → trusted → revoke lifecycle with 8/8 checks in both eligibility modes. Decoupling the scheduler from veriﬁcation is what bounds unvetted exposure under backlog: under 50 × backlog, decoupled scheduling gave Eu ≈ Tp versus 50 Tp under coupled scheduling. On the Milvus Lite real-time control plane, Eu was 1.00 Tp decoupled versus ≈5 Tp coupled under a ∼5 s backlog. B.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: B. Retrieval-layer poisoning exposure and clean-content cost Poison crafted against a designated query set is injected into a collection held loaded throughout, with eligibility on the post-ﬁlter path, and we measure what each baseline lets it do (Fig. 2): ﬁve independently generated workloads whose synthetic corpora keep exact eligible-neighbor ground truth computable; Sec. VII-C repeats the grid on encoded naturallanguage documents. Three query sets separate what one poisoned-retrieval rate conﬂates. The set Qcraft, the queries the poison was optimized against, is a worst case by construction; Qtgt holds disjoint queries of the same topic, so a hit there is transfer; Qneg is unrelated. Rates are reported over the queries B1 compromised, a set applied unchanged to every baseline and Tp; counts are unaffected by that conditioning.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: Rates are reported over the queries B1 compromised, a set applied unchanged to every baseline and Tp; counts are unaffected by that conditioning. The poison reached 75–100% of crafted queries, while transfer was partial: it reached 12–38% of disjoint sametopic queries, with every workload showing some transfer, and produced no poisoned retrieval on any of the 40 distinct unrelated queries. Whether a query retrieves poison is decided by the best poison it can see against its own top-5 cutoff, so we report that pairing rather than an average over unrelated pairs: for the median target query the best poison falls 0 .037– 0.061 short of the cutoff, and yet 1–3 of each workload’s eight queries clear it. Predicted and retrieved agree for every one of the 80 held-out queries across both workloads (Sec. VII-C), so the transfer rate is a property of the geometry, not of the defense or of when a query happened to run.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: VII-C), so the transfer rate is a property of the geometry, not of the defense or of when a query happened to run. Under backlog, the deadline rather than veriﬁcation ended exposure (Table I). B1 never contains the poison; its exposure window ends only when measurement stops. B3 holds at B1’s rate for 4 .7 s until veriﬁcation drains, and B4 is cut at the deadline; the conditional rates are 0 .57–0.63 for B3 and 0.125 for B4, versus 0 .875 for B1. Counts and rates are both per-workload medians over workloads whose qualiﬁed-query counts differ, so the rate is not the ratio of the counts. When the veriﬁer keeps up, the two are indistinguishable, because veriﬁcation commits inside Tp and the deadline never binds: the deadline is what makes the bound survive backlog, not what creates it. This reduction came with a clean-content trade-off.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: This reduction came with a clean-content trade-off. V erifybefore-visible delays clean ﬁrst visibility until veriﬁcation completes: 0 .62 s with the veriﬁer keeping up, 6 .3 s under backlog. The appropriate policy depends on application requirements: a security-sensitive deployment can shorten Tp; provisioning veriﬁcation to commit before expiry reduces gaps under expected load; and an application that cannot tolerate gaps after ﬁrst visibility should use verifybefore-visible and accept its initial freshness delay. Lengthening Tp reduces expiry risk only by widening the unvettedvisibility budget. The deadline does not reduce a poison’s effect while it remains visible: relative to the clean top- k that would have been returned without the poison, the poison displaced 20% of clean results under B1, B3, and B4 alike, and eligible retrieval returned the exact top- k after containment. Per-hit displacement was therefore identical across the three; only duration, and hence the cumulative ﬁgure, differs. Exposure scales with the budget, so Tp is a calibrated dial rather than a qualitative switch.

text: The corpus becomes 600 posts from eight 20 Newsgroups categories spanning recreation, science, computing, politics, religion and commerce, 75 each, with headers, footers and quoted replies stripped, encoded by all- MiniLM-L6-v2 at 384 dimensions; queries are the opening words of held-out posts, leaving Qcraft and Qtgt disjoint real utterances. The poison is an English passage inspired by PoisonedRAG’s black-box query-repetition construction [6]: our implementation repeats the target query, appends ﬁxed assertive ﬁller and tests whether the result enters the encoder’s top-k without manual vector-space placement. It does not instantiate PoisonedRAG’s target-answer generation condition. The attack survives the substitution. Judged by the same per-query top-5 cutoff rule, the poison falls 0 .034–0.093 short for the median target query, and 1–3 of each workload’s eight clear it anyway. Poison was retrieved for 12–38% of these queries, with at least one transfer in every workload, but for none of the 40 distinct unrelated queries.

Together, these observations support attributing transfer to the encoded geometry rather than query opportunity. The right-hand column of Table I shows the same baseline ordering: B3 degrades under backlog while B4 holds at the deadline, the two are indistinguishable when the veriﬁer keeps up, and exposure remains monotone in the budget. title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: We next replace the oracle with controlled and measured detector outcomes. In the controlled sweep, B4 was conﬁgured to falsely promote k = 0, 1, 2, 3 items: B1 stayed at 49 median poisoned retrievals, while B4 rose from 7 to 9, 13 and 15, with every observed provisional exposure below 1 .02 s. On 512 held-out source groups, D1’s TP/FP/TN/FN counts were 129/65/255/63; recall was 125/128 for the matched recipe but 4/64 for the predeﬁned natural-cover-sufﬁx cross-attack, while 65/320 clean items were falsely refused. Detector-only P50, P95, and P99 latencies were 26.1, 37.7, and 49.8 ms, respectively. Each 300-admission HNSW replay produced 38 false promotions and 29 false refusals. All 38 false promotions remained visible at the window end under B2–B4; B2 never exposed false-refused clean items, whereas B3/B4 exposed them brieﬂy and excluded them from retrieval by the window end. The deadline bounds provisional exposure but cannot revoke poison after promotion. D.

text: D. Eligibility enforcement and top-k completeness V alues below are means across three seeds; each seed’s P95, under-ﬁll rate and recall are computed separately before aggregation. At 30% global hidden occupancy with 2 × overfetch, clustered hiding raised the P95 candidate-pool hidden occupancy from 0 .47 to 0 .58 and under-ﬁll from 0 .7% to 8% at an unchanged median hM of 0 .30; the query-coupled stress construction gave 26%. At 1 × over-fetch, Eligible Recall@ k was 0 .70, 0 .68 and 0 .38 under uniform, clustered and querycoupled hiding. At 4 ×, observed under-ﬁll was eliminated and recall reached 1 .0 in all three. Conditional Recall@ k was 1.0 wherever a full- k result existed and is undeﬁned for the query-coupled 1 × cell, which produced none, so recall loss follows from under-ﬁll rather than selection error. The in-index ﬁlter returned the exact eligible top- k wherever the eligible population stayed ≥ k. Over-fetch is not free.

text: Over-fetch is not free. At 4 ×, each query requests four times as many candidates as at 1 ×, so candidate transfer and post-ﬁlter checks increase; the backendspeciﬁc effects on ANN search cost and latency were not measured. Because α never relaxes the authoritative eligibility check, operators should use the smallest α that meets their completeness target for the observed upper tail of hM, or use in-index ﬁltering when its propagation delay and consistency semantics are acceptable. The 4 × result demonstrates completeness for these workloads, not zero deployment cost. E. Milvus Lite functional validation On Milvus Lite, the adapter, all four state paths and both eligibility modes execute against a real Milvus API and reproduce the trends above. Conditional Recall@ k was 1.0 because the FLA T index adds no ANN approximation. F .

text: F . Lineage-scoped containment In the evaluated revocation workload, lineage-scoped containment caught 100% of the poison at all three granularities, while collateral removal fell from ∼83% (by source) to ∼43% (by batch) to 0% at exact item-lineage granularity. At equal poison recall, these ﬁgures quantify the collateral cost of each scope choice and the reduction in collateral removal when alert evidence supports a narrower scope; they do not identify a universally optimal granularity. Through the post-ﬁlter path, no residual retrieval followed logical revocation on either backend. Through the in-index path, it persisted immediately after the scalar update on Milvus Lite ( ∼29–48% of probes), so that path propagates a hide with nonzero delay (Sec. VI-C). G. Standalone system results We ﬁrst conduct a single-run propagation microbenchmark on Milvus Standalone v2.4.15 (single node, Docker) [9] over a 200-item collection of synthetic unit vectors and measure the in-index mode’s δhide end to end.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: Standalone system results We ﬁrst conduct a single-run propagation microbenchmark on Milvus Standalone v2.4.15 (single node, Docker) [9] over a 200-item collection of synthetic unit vectors and measure the in-index mode’s δhide end to end. The delay δhide is computed from deadline expiry per the logged timestamps; probing begins at acknowledgment. Two probes run concurrently: a scalar point lookup and an exact (FLA T) top- k search. FLA T is used because under an approximate index a vanished item cannot be distinguished from a recall miss; concurrency keeps either probe’s service time from being charged to the other. The grid is four read-consistency levels × {no, heavy} backlog, Tp = 1 s, 200 hide events per cell, with an identical control cell at the start and end of the run; we report δhide as a conservative upper bound derived from interval censoring (Sec. VI-A).

text: VI-A). The hide is an override upsert because v2.4.15 has no in-place scalar update, so the magnitudes are properties of that update path as well as of the protocol. Read consistency determined whether completed probes remained stale after the hide committed. Under Strong and Session, no completed probe returned the item in any cell: 0 stale reads out of 200 events per cell. Under Bounded and Eventually, provisional items stayed retrievable across dozens of completed probes. In the Bounded and Eventually cells δhide was 288–332 ms at P50 and 380–431 ms at P95; the 9–12 ms censoring bracket means that the reported bounds overstate the true delay by at most ∼12 ms. Under Strong and Session, the probe itself costs ∼420 ms at P95, so the ﬁrst completed probe already reports the item hidden and δhide is bounded but never point-estimated. That 420 ms characterizes the instrument, not the underlying delay, which may be identical across modes.

Adding the scalar probe added no material cost to the top- k search path under this workload (P95 421.0 ms with it versus 419.7 ms without), so these delays are not an instrumentation artifact. Thus δhide must be budgeted: at Tp = 1 s, a P95 enforcement delay of ∼0.43 s widens the worst-case unvetted-exposure window by more than 40%. That magnitude belongs to the in-index scalar-update path, not to the control-store post-ﬁlter conﬁguration of Sec. VII-B. The panel cannot identify a veriﬁer-backlog effect. Its two control cells perform identical query-only work at the run’s start and end, yet their P50 values differ by 22.3 ms (6.5%), a shift that exceeds the between-cell effects.

We therefore report rounded magnitudes and categorical behavior only: where δhide resolved, the backlog contrast changed sign (Bounded +50 ms, Eventually −23 ms), and both magnitudes were of the same order as the control drift. With 200 events per cell, the panel supports median estimation; P95 is tail-limited, and P99 is not reported. We report ﬁve Milvus process runs that passed ﬁxed validity gates; the artifact retains all attempts. Each run built a 100,000vector HNSW index using cosine similarity [11], with M = 16, efConstruction=200, and Strong consistency. Each run used the same ﬁxed set of 192 queries. At the primary ef=64 setting, run-level median Recall@5 was 0.9979 (range 0.9979– 0.9990), median P95 latency was 0.412 s, and no query errors occurred.
