text: At the primary ef=64 setting, run-level median Recall@5 was 0.9979 (range 0.9979– 0.9990), median P95 latency was 0.412 s, and no query errors occurred. With 20 admissions/s, median throughput across the four admission policies increased from 3.27–3.33 queries per second (QPS) at concurrency 1 to 48.0–51.27 QPS at concurrency 16, with no admission failures. Median P95 query latency at concurrency 16 was 0.408–0.416 s. VIII. R ELATED WORK Corpus-poisoning attacks can steer dense retrieval with a small injected set [5], and PoisonedRAG extends the threat to attacker-chosen generation [6]. We propose no new attack. SilentRetrieval studies ﬂuent, semantics-preserving variants of such poisoning [7]. Our threat model admits this adversary (Sec. II-A). RAGuard ﬁlters suspicious retrieved chunks [12], and PRA- RAG robustly aggregates retrieved evidence [13]. Orchestration and forensics complement such ﬁltering. ADO selects defenses per query context [14], and RAGForensics traces harmful outputs to responsible passages [15].

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: ADO selects defenses per query context [14], and RAGForensics traces harmful outputs to responsible passages [15]. These studies predominantly use static or batch-constructed corpora and report method-speciﬁc outcomes rather than temporal exposure, containment and recovery under continuous ingestion. In-toto formalizes software-supply-chain attestation for how an artifact was produced [16], and RAGShield applies provenance checks to RAG ingestion and shows their insufﬁciency against a valid-key insider [8]. The latter result motivates our multi-signal rule without prescribing a detector. Milvus provides similarity search over mutable collections [9], and Manu develops a cloud-native vector-DBMS architecture [10]. Our control store holds only eligibility state beside such a system (Sec. V). FreshDiskANN supports incremental updates of a graph index [17], while SPFresh performs in-place updates without full rebuilds [18]. Freshness has also been pursued at the RAG layer. Streaming RAG incrementally refreshes a compact prototype index [3], and SPI adapts retrieval resolution per query [19]. Temporal retrieval is a further direction.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: Temporal retrieval is a further direction. LiveV ectorLake adds versioned point-in-time retrieval [4]. These systems optimize freshness, update efﬁciency or temporal retrieval but do not model adversarial exposure windows. A recent RAG-security survey separates admission-time integrity, retrieval-time hardening and post-retrieval mitigation [20]. Our focus is the temporal ingestion-to-retrieval lifecycle under concurrent updates. IX. L IMITATIONS The Eu ≤ Tp + δhide bound inherits the deployment’s enforcement delay. The corresponding Ep bound holds only absent false promotion; falsely promoted items require later containment. V erify-before-visible avoids provisional exposure at higher freshness delay, and a deadline limits exposure duration rather than damage per retrieval. Accordingly, the protocol controls unvetted-visibility duration; it does not solve poisoning detection. Hard gates assume an honest control plane; post-ﬁltering requires over-fetch; distributed clocks and rollback remain out of scope. D1 is one recipe-speciﬁc detector evaluated on 512 held-out source groups.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: D1 is one recipe-speciﬁc detector evaluated on 512 held-out source groups. Its matched-recipe and cross-attack results do not establish detector generality, unknown-attack robustness or second-detector replication, and ofﬂine replay excludes inference contention. The real-text study ends at retrieval rather than answer generation. Physical-purge latency, storage overhead while hidden vectors remain in the index, and restore or reindex behavior were not evaluated. The Standalone propagation panel is a single-run measurement of the in-index update path; a second-host replication passed its ﬁxed stability gate in only two of ﬁve runs and therefore contributes no latency estimate. The ﬁve HNSW runs are single-node measurements, and 98,248 of 100,000 vectors are deterministic pressure data. Requests are not independent statistical units; QPS and latency tails do not establish production capacity, availability, fault tolerance, or distributed scaling. Milvus Lite and cross-backend results validate implementation consistency, not independent performance replication. X. C ONCLUSION Continuous RAG ingestion creates distinct unvetted- and poisoning-exposure intervals.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
text: C ONCLUSION Continuous RAG ingestion creates distinct unvetted- and poisoning-exposure intervals. The protocol bounds the ﬁrst by a deadline plus query-path enforcement delay and supports lineage-scoped containment; on encoded natural-language workloads under backlog it cut poisoned retrievals and displaced clean results by roughly a factor of ﬁve, while clean availability could lapse. D1’s false promotions and refusals show why the poison bound is conditional and why detector quality has a clean-content cost. Five single-node HNSW runs show high-recall ANN retrieval under concurrent ingestion for this workload. title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Agentic AI is emerging as a promising paradigm for automating complex cybersecurity decisions, yet its use in enforcing zero trust introduces significant challenges in safety, reliability, and policy compliance. This paper presents Agentic AI based zero trust architecture (Agentic-ZTA) that operationalizes the NIST SP 800-207 ZTA architecture control loop through coordinated multi- agent decision pipeline. In the proposed framework, policy knowledge is embedded into a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline and retrieved at inference time as top-k relevant policies. Access requests are intercepted by the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), enriched with contextual metadata. The request context is routed to a policy engine agent which invokes domain-specialized core agents first followed by supporting agents, if further evaluation needed. AI agents reason over access context, policy constraints and determine trust. The retrieved policies are embedded into agent prompt during inference time and agentic trust scores are aggregated and evaluated by a trust-algorithm, producing the final access decision for enforcement under continuous verification. We implement Agentic-ZTA in a testbed and evaluate it on representative access-control use cases scenarios. Our Agentic-ZTA framework achieves 95.0% accuracy, 93.9% precision, and 96.3% recall, and demonstrate the feasibility of enforcing zero trust using AI agents.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Zero trust architecture (ZTA) [1] is an approach to cybersecurity based on the principle “never trust, always verify”. It is intended to remove the implicit trust in users, services, and devices based only on their network location, affiliation, and ownership. Zero trust focuses on protecting resources (e.g., devices, services, workflows, network accounts) through least privilege, fine grained access control and dynamic policy update [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. ZTA enforces secure authorized access to enterprise resources while continually inspecting, monitoring, and logging interactions with users, devices, applications, and data across networks and workloads[7]. To realize these principles in practice, NIST defines a set of logical components that collectively evaluate, authorize, and enforce access requests. According to the NIST SP 800-207 [1], Zero Trust Architecture is composed of three logical components: the Policy Decision Point (PDP), the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), and the Policy Information Point (PIP).

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: According to the NIST SP 800-207 [1], Zero Trust Architecture is composed of three logical components: the Policy Decision Point (PDP), the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), and the Policy Information Point (PIP). The PDP serves as the central decision making component and determines whether to allow or deny a request. Specifically, its Policy Engine (PE) evaluates requests against defined policies, contextual telemetry, and trust Email addresses:sroy42@tntech.edu(Shovan Roy), lopamudra.praharaj@uncp.edu(Lopamudra Praharaj), mgupta@tntech.edu(Maanak Gupta), bhavani.thuraisingham@utdallas.edu(Bhavani Thuraisingham) attributes. The PEP acts as the enforcement mechanism positioned between the subject and the resource. All access requests pass through the PEP, which communicates with the PDP for an authorization decision before allowing, denying or terminating a session. PIPs serve as supporting data sources that supply the PDP with real-time contextual and security telemetry required for informed evaluations.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: PIPs serve as supporting data sources that supply the PDP with real-time contextual and security telemetry required for informed evaluations. These sources include identity management systems, compliance, Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), threat intelligence platforms, Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems, data access policies, Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation (CDM) systems, and network and activity logs. Collectively, these components enable ZTA to continuously evaluate access requests based on identity, device posture, security context, and enterprise policies [1]. Prior to the adoption of Zero Trust, traditional cybersecurity architectures primarily relied on perimeter-based security, where users and devices located within the organizational network were implicitly trusted. Access decisions were largely based on network location, IP addresses, or predefined security zones. However, with the explosion of cloud computing and hybrid work, the perimeter no longer exists. Corporate data no longer sits in a single physical data center.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Corporate data no longer sits in a single physical data center. Employees access company resources from home networks, coffee shops, and personal devices, meaning there is no longer a clear "inside" to protect. Zero Trust is essential because it secures access regardless of location, device, or network, making it the viable arXiv:2610.05782v1 [cs.AI] 5 Oct 2026 model for today’s complex, distributed IT ecosystems. Zero Trust replaces implicit trust with continuous verification and least-privilege access. The use of machine learning (ML) in ZTA has significantly expedited cybersecurity tasks such as detection of network intrusion, malware, phishing, anomaly detection, identification of unusual network traffic and log analysis [8, 9, 10]. ML algorithms leverage historical data to detect patterns that may indicate potential security breaches [4]. Machine learning based access control systems ranging from simple classifiers such as SVMs[11] and random forests[12, 13] to deep learning like DLBAC [14] replace manual policy rules to make allow/deny decisions[15].

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Machine learning based access control systems ranging from simple classifiers such as SVMs[11] and random forests[12, 13] to deep learning like DLBAC [14] replace manual policy rules to make allow/deny decisions[15]. However, these approaches operate as black boxes: they lack the reasoning needed to understand why an event occurs. As a result, they fail to provide human-readable justifications or explainable rationales for their decisions, making it difficult to audit them in Zero Trust environments. Large language models are increasingly used to make access control decisions directly rather than only mining or generating policies. Rubio-Medrano et al. pair LLMs with formal policy specifications so that access decisions remain traceable[16]. Cheng et al. propose LACE, a retrieval-augmented framework where an LLM reasons over relevant policy context to determine IoT access decisions[17]. Similarly, Zisad and Hasan finetune a Mistral 7B model to unify RBAC, ABAC, and DAC into a single LLM-based decision layer [18].

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Similarly, Zisad and Hasan finetune a Mistral 7B model to unify RBAC, ABAC, and DAC into a single LLM-based decision layer [18]. However, these systems stop at the decision itself: they output allow/deny with an explanation, but no subsequent mechanism auto-enforces that decision, revokes access if conditions change, or re-validates the session while it remains active which goes against Zero Trust’s principle of continuous verification [1]. Nonetheless, Zero trust enforcement based on LLM misses the autonomous characteristics, i.e. it cannot initiate action independently and cannot coordinate complex, multi-step process without human interaction [19, 20]. To the best of our knowledge there is currently no framework that integrate Agentic AI into the Policy Decision Point (PDP) which can autonomously enforce Zero Trust access control decision. Agentic AI, is the artificial intelligence systems that can autonomously make decisions and take actions to pursue complex goals with minimum or no human intervention [21, 22, 23, 24].

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Agentic AI, is the artificial intelligence systems that can autonomously make decisions and take actions to pursue complex goals with minimum or no human intervention [21, 22, 23, 24]. Agentic AI is used in Zero Trust access control to support continuous trust evaluation, context-aware authorization, and autonomous response. It can analyze identity, device posture, behavioral, and environmental signals and initiate actions such as privilege reduction, token revocation, or device isolation. These capabilities improve least-privilege enforcement, threat response, policy adaptation, and scalability in dynamic environments such as Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT)[25] , where heterogeneous devices, changing mission conditions, intermittent connectivity, and evolving cyber threats require rapid and adaptive access-control decisions. In addition, Retrieval- Augmented Generation (RAG) [26] can reduce hallucinations and reliance on obsolete policy information by grounding the LLM’s responses in a retrievable and verifiable knowledge base. This retrieved policy specific context generate more accurate and up-to-date authorization decision.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Allowdecision, Agent can take actions like issue access token, log the decision for audit, and notify the requester by invoking tools. Upon a Denydecision, Agent can take actions like revoke certificate, isolate session along with logging the decision and notifying the requester. This paper is motivated by three foundational research questions: •RQ1:Can LLM-based AI agents autonomously enforce a NIST Zero Trust requirements and policies with sufficient accuracy? •RQ2:Can LLM-based agents produce decisions that are auditable and accountable enough to trust the autonomous enforcement? •RQ3:Is the inference latency introduced by multi-agent orchestration low enough to permit real-time Zero Trust enforcement without degrading decision accuracy? Table 1 compares the most closely related prior work across six capability dimensions relevant to autonomous zero-trust enforcement, rating each as full support (+), partial support (◦), or no support (–). The comparison reveals four compound limitations that no single prior system addresses simultaneously. L1:Static Policy Evaluation:All surveyed ZTA systems operate with static policy rules.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: L1:Static Policy Evaluation:All surveyed ZTA systems operate with static policy rules. No system dynamically synthesizes enforceable policies at inference time. Novel or composite attack patterns therefore evade detection until the policy base is manually updated. L2:Ungrounded LLM Reasoning:Prior work that support LLM generated reasoning but no way to check the reasoning behind it. None of these systems ground the model’s reasoning from a policy knowledge base, so the LLM can produce a response that sounds reasonable but has no real evidence behind it. L3:Lake of Autonomous Action:LLM-based systems produce detection or classification outputs but do not enforce action autonomously. The resulting architectures require a human analyst or a separate, manually configured enforcement system to translate decision into PEP actions. L4:Lack of Implementation:Most reviewed systems present conceptual frameworks or partial prototypes without 2 demonstrating a working implementation.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: L4:Lack of Implementation:Most reviewed systems present conceptual frameworks or partial prototypes without 2 demonstrating a working implementation. Only three works [2, 7, 29] report partial implementations, and none deploy a complete autonomous ZTA pipeline integrating multi-agent orchestration, RAG-grounded reasoning, and continuous validation. This paper addresses all four limitations, as it integrates a NIST-aligned PDP-PEP enforcement loop with multiple agents. It takes decisions and autonomously enforce them (L1andL3). It grounds each agent’s reasoning in RAG-retrieved policy evidence (L2), and is validated through the implementation on a testbed (L4). The key contributions to this work are as follows:

Section 6 reports the experimental evaluation. Section 7 discusses future research. Section 8 concludes. 2 Background and Related Work. 2.1 Zero Trust Architecture. Zero trust architecture (ZTA) [1] is an approach to cybersecurity based on the principle “never trust, always verify”. Its intended to remove the implicit trust in users, services, and devices based only on their network location, affiliation, and ownership. Zero trust focuses on protecting resources (e.g., devices, services, workflows, network accounts) through least privilege, per-session basis fine grained access control and dynamic policy update [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. ZTA enforce risk-based access controls while continually inspect, monitor, and log interactions [7].

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
section: 4 We showcase the practical application of our proposed
text: ZTA enforce risk-based access controls while continually inspect, monitor, and log interactions [7]. According to NIST ZTA, there are some core components including the policy engine which evaluates access requests using a trust algorithm, policy administrator translate decision into enforceable actions. Supporting sources such as identity systems, threat intelligence, SIEM, network and activity logs provide real time inputs to determine access decisions. Consequently, ZTA has become the dominant access-control paradigm for enterprise, cloud, and operational environments, codified in U.S. federal policy and adopted across regulated industries[1, 30, 31]. Its core requirement is: every access request must be authenticated, authorized, and continuously reevaluated through a Policy Decision Point (PDP) and Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) control loop, with no trust granted implicitly on the basis of network location or prior authorization state[1].

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: A growing body of work replaces language-based access control policies with trained ML models for access control decision making, rather than using ML to assist policy mining, verification, testing administration, monitoring and auditing [15]. Nobi et al.[15] survey this line of work under the name ML-based access control (MLBAC). Chang et al. proposed a time-constrained access control system using SVMs trained on login-time and password features to classify users and grant access [11]. Outchakoucht et al. combined blockchain-based policy management with reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust IoT access control policies [32]. Cappelletti et al. compared symbolic (decision tree, random forest) and non-symbolic (support vector classifier, multi-layer perceptron) ML for inferring ABAC access decisions from access logs[33]. Similarly, Khilar et al. evaluated an ensemble of random forest andk-nearest-neighbor classifiers for trust-based cloud resource access decisions[13], and Srivastava et al. proposed a risk-adaptive access control framework using neural networks and random forests to assess requester genuineness[34].

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Similarly, Khilar et al. evaluated an ensemble of random forest andk-nearest-neighbor classifiers for trust-based cloud resource access decisions[13], and Srivastava et al. proposed a risk-adaptive access control framework using neural networks and random forests to assess requester genuineness[34]. Liu et al. improved the ABAC policy decision point directly with a random-forest-based permission decision engine[12], while Karimi et al. applied reinforcement learning to adaptive ABAC policy learning under sparse-log conditions[35]. Deep Learning Based Access Control (DLBAC) replaces attribute and policy engineering with a ResNet-based neural network trained directly on user and resource metadata[14]. Notably, none of these access-decision approaches employ large language models. The use of LLM-based agents for zero trust access decision-making extends this line of work beyond the classical and deep-learning methods.

text: Lewis et al.[26] demonstrated that augmenting LLM generation with differentiable retrieval substantially reduces hallucination, establishing RAG as a viable approach for security policy grounding where factual accuracy is strictly required. However, in their survey of LLM security vulnerabilities, Yao et al.[36] identified non-reproducibility across invocations and hallucination under adversarial inputs as the primary failure modes in auditable enforcement layers. Agentic-ZTA directly mitigates these non-reproducibility risks through two deterministic mechanisms: fixed top-kvector retrieval over the policy knowledge base and greedy decoding (temperature=0) across all agent inference calls. This combination ensures that context retrieval remains stable for identical inputs while eliminating stochastic variance during policy evaluation. 3

section: 2.4 Multi-Agent Systems for Autonomous Cyber Defense
text: Multi-agent systems (MAS) distribute reasoning and operational tasks across specialized autonomous agents, each maintaining domain-specific operational contexts[27]. In cybersecurity, MAS architectures have been applied to intrusion detection[37], network traffic classification, and automated incident response. Early designs relied heavily on static rule engines, which subsequent works replaced with reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-agent RL (MARL) algorithms[29]. However, RL-based approaches exhibit critical drawbacks in security-sensitive deployments: formulating well-calibrated reward functions is challenging, sparse feedback delays training convergence and learned policies frequently fail to generalize against unseen attack scenarios[38, 39]. More recently, Deng et al.[28] surveyed vulnerabilities specific to LLM-driven agent deployments, identifying prompt injection, knowledge-base poisoning, and orchestration-layer hijacking as primary threat vectors. Agentic-ZTA mitigates knowledge-base poisoning and hallucination by enforcing domain-specific, policy-grounded vector retrieval. Each agent’s contextual inputs strictly to authoritative, verified telemetry. Beyond reasoning quality, separation of duties constitutes a foundational security rationale for multi-agent architectures.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
section: 2.4 Multi-Agent Systems for Autonomous Cyber Defense
text: Beyond reasoning quality, separation of duties constitutes a foundational security rationale for multi-agent architectures. In access control, no single autonomous component should possess unilateral authority to allow access, preserving an essential principle first formalized in RBAC systems to prevent fraud and single-point compromise[40, 41]. Agentic-ZTA enforces this separation directly within its orchestration workflow. Discrete operational checks including identity verification (IAM), cryptographic validation (PKI), behavioral anomaly tracking (SIEM), and policy checkes (Data Access Policy) are decoupled into specialized autonomous agents, each grounded in its dedicated RAG pipeline. To ensure default deny policy, any core agentDENYverdict triggers immediate enforcement by the PEP, bypassing subsequent trust evaluation. In contrast, anALLOWverdict requires multi-agent consensus through formal trust fusion. Consequently, a compromised agent can at worst result in a denial of service, but can never unilaterally allow unauthorized access.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Agentic-ZTA (Fig.1) separates the control plane from the data plane, adhering to the NIST SP 800-207 reference architecture[1]. The control plane hosts the Policy Decision Point (PDP), wherein the Policy Engine (PE) agent operates as the central orchestrator. It does not itself hold domain knowledge, identity records, certificates, threat signatures instead it receives the access request, decides which agents to invoke, collects their assessments and provides the final access decision applying trust algorithm. We structure the evaluation agents into two tiers based on decision authority:core agentsandsupporting agents. Acore agentpossesses authoritative power: a negative assessment terminates the agentic evaluation immediately, aborting further agent queries and bypassing trust algorithm. The Identity Management (IAM) Agent,Threat Detection Agent, and Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Agentserve as core agents. They map to the identity, credential, and threat dimensions that NIST designates as non-negotiable trust primitives for any PDP[1].

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: They map to the identity, credential, and threat dimensions that NIST designates as non-negotiable trust primitives for any PDP[1]. If any of the core agents decides on aDENY, the PE agent instructs the PEP to enforce an immediate denial action. Conversely, asupporting agentprovides auxiliary contextual telemetry such as compliance posture, policy fit or log anomalies that feeds into the confidence-weighted trust score, but its output alone cannot unilaterally force aDENY. TheData Access Policy Agent,Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) Agent,Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation (CDM) Agent,Compliance Agent, andActivity and Log Monitoring Agentconstitute this tier. Supporting agents are invoked only when all core agents have issued anALLOW. The data plane hosts the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), which mediates all communication between the subject and the protected resources. The user resides in theuntrusted zonei.e. no request is trusted. The PEP shields the resources blocking all traffic until the control plane (PDP) evaluates the request.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: The PEP shields the resources blocking all traffic until the control plane (PDP) evaluates the request. Once the PE Agent returns an ALLOW decision, the PEP grants ephemeral access strictly to the requested endpoint under granular micro-segmentation, preserving strict isolation between resources. While access remains active, the PE Agent continuously re-evaluates the session and revokes access through the PEP if an anomaly is detected. The operational workflow has been explain in details in section 3.2. A continuous validation loop operates concurrently with this workflow. Throughout an active session, the PE agent periodically re-evaluates trust attributes using real-time inputs from both core and supporting agents, ensuring persistent compliance rather than relying on a static, one-time check.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: 3.1.1 Orchestrator Agent:. Policy Engine (PE) Agent: The PE Agent is the principal decision-maker in the Agentic-ZTA framework and acts as the soleorchestrator agent. It is responsible for allowing or denying access to enterprise resources through continuous risk assessment and trust evaluation. The PE Agent first invokes the subset from the core agents (ID Management, PKI, Threat Detection). If any of the core agents returns a DENY , the PE Agent finalizes the decision as DENY and take corresponding actions immediately, without invoking the supporting agents. Otherwise, the PE Agent invokes the subset from the supporting agents (Data Access Policy, SIEM, CDM, Compliance, Activity and Logs Monitoring) and ingests their trust scores, confidence scores, and reasoning alongside the core agents’ assessments. These assessments are fed into Algorithm 1 to compute a confidence-weighted trust scoreT, which is compared against the destination zone’s trust thresholdτ z to reach a final ALLOW or DENY decision.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: 5.1 IoBT Scenario Context. The scenario in Figure 3 reflects an Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT), a heterogeneous environment in which a wide range of sensors, devices, vehicles, soldier wearables, and command systems collaborate to accomplish mission objectives under contested conditions [45, 25]. In IoBT coalition operation multiple nations and partners share battlefield information to accomplish mission goal while still protecting their own security rules, data classifications. The testbed models five zones:Nation A Tactical,Nation B Tactical,Mission HQ,Mission Partner, and a centralShared Data Fabricthat serves as the coalition exchange hub. Nation A Tactical networkrepresents one nation’s frontline battlefield enclave. It contains heterogeneous edge devices such as unmanned aerial vehicles (UA Vs), unattended ground sensors (UGS), unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) and soldier wearables, along with edge processor, MQTT hub and Command and Control (C2) server. These devices constantly generate telemetry such as position, health status, reconnaissance feeds and mission alerts. Raw battlefield data is first collected here.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Raw battlefield data is first collected here. These devices often operate with limited bandwidth, low energy, and limited connectivity. The MQTT broker supports local communication among devices, the edge processor performs initial preprocessing and filtering, and the C2 server integrates the resulting data before publishing the consolidated information to the shared data fabric. Nation B Tacticalis a separate sovereign tactical enclave with a similar structure, but its own policies, priorities, and trust rules. Even though it participates in the same coalition mission, it does not automatically trust other zones or accept access requests. This is because coalition partners may have different kinds of intelligence, but each nation still has to decide what can be shared, what must remain local, and what requires extra protection. Mission HQacts as the coalition command and intelligence center. It receives consolidated telemetry from the tactical zones, fuses the data into a broader mission picture and sends mission commands back to tactical operators.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: It receives consolidated telemetry from the tactical zones, fuses the data into a broader mission picture and sends mission commands back to tactical operators. Mission HQ must make sure that the information it receives is trusted and that the commands it sends stay within mission and policy boundary. Mission Partnerrepresents allied or coalition partner forces that support the mission but may not have the same level of access as the tactical zones- Nation A and Nation B. These nodes are allowed to receive processed intelligence that is relevant to their assigned tasks, but raw sensor telemetry is still controlled by coalition releasability rules. Coalition data sharing is selective, conditional, and based on mission need. TheShared Data Fabricis the central exchange point that connects all of the zones. It is not just a storage layer or a data relay. In this architecture, it is the place where coalition data is checked, filtered, and controlled before being shared across boundaries.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: In this architecture, it is the place where coalition data is checked, filtered, and controlled before being shared across boundaries. All inter-zone traffic passes through this fabric, and the exchange happens over HTTPS so that communication remains protected while still allowing controlled sharing. Thousands of requests may arrive from sensors, vehicles, operators, commanders, and coalition partners. Each request may depend on the current mission phase, device health, network condition, and threat level. A rule-based system alone is too rigid for this environment because it cannot adapt quickly enough when devices move, credentials are compromised, or a mission priority suddenly changes. In this scenario Agentic- ZTA is necessary: it gives the system an autonomous decision layer that can continuously evaluate who is requesting, what they want, whether the device or user is trustworthy, and whether the request fits the current mission and coalition policy. Agentic-ZTA system is deployed at the Shared Data Fabric. Agentic-ZTA system is deployed at the Shared Data Fabric. Each zone’s gateway acts as a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) that intercepts every access request, add metadata and forwards it to the Policy Engine (PE) Agent for decision.

text: 6.1 Testbed and Deployment. To demonstrate Agentic-ZTA in a representative operational setting, we deployed 5 zoned IoBT testbed across Linux virtual 12 Figure 4: Agentic actions executed by the PE Agent following the trust decision. OnAllow, the PE Agent callsissue_access_token(), log_decision()andsend_notification()tools. OnDeny, it calls revoke_certificate(),quarantine_session(),log_decision()and send_notification()tools. machines. This is a VM-based arrangement with isolated network to represent Nation-A, Nation-B, Mission HQ, Mission Partner and shared data fabric. Nation A further implemented an MQTT broker, an edge processor, a C2 server all are containers. All IoBT devices e.g. UA V , UGV , Soldier are simulated. The UA V client publishes GPS, camera, and radio telemetry as JSON messages, while the ground sensor client publishes motion, acoustic, seismic, pressure, environmental, and device-health observations. Nation B has a separate MQTT broker and corresponding edge and C2 services, as well as an unmanned ground vehicle and an intelligence consumer. Mission HQ and other coalition entities are represented by MQTT consumers.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Mission HQ and other coalition entities are represented by MQTT consumers. The Mission HQ command publisher can also generate strategic commands for Coalition Tactical Operators (CTOs) in Nation B using MQTT publisher. MQTT is used as the asynchronous transport between devices, brokers, processing services, and consumers. Device messages are published on sensor-specific topics, edge services subscribe and processed messages are forwarded to C2 topics. The C2 service converts telemetry into intelligence records and publishes them to the Shared Data Fabric. The clients use QoS 2 for sensor, command, and intelligence messages. TLS is available as a deployment option, when enabled, the clients load the CA certificate. The Shared Data Fabric acts as the distribution point for intelligence and commands. It subscribes to intelligence and CTO command topics and publishes intelligence to consumerspecific topics. Commands received from Mission HQ are forwarded to the Nation B CTO through a second MQTT broker connection.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: Commands received from Mission HQ are forwarded to the Nation B CTO through a second MQTT broker connection. The requests are submitted over HTTP to the PE Agent, which orchestrates the specialized agents and returns anALLOW orDENYoutcome. A denial can therefore prevent telemetry from continuing through the relevant processing path, while an allowed message is processed and distributed through the MQTT fabric.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: All experiments were executed in a Linux environment using a self-hosted Ollama endpoint. Ollama was installed and run locally on the testbed machine, serving the LLM (Llama 3.1) over a local endpoint. The current implementation uses a single shared LLM backend for all agents rather than separate models or per-agent instances. Specialization is achieved through agent-specific prompts, tool bindings, and isolated ChromaDB policy collections. Policies are stored in per-agent collections forIAM,PKI,Threat Detection,CDM,Data Access Policy,SIEM, andActivity and Logs Monitoring. Each agent retrieves up to the top-5 matching rules from its own collection during inference. The PE agent evaluates the invoked core agents first and terminates immediately if any core agent returnsDENY. If all core agents allow the request, the supporting agents are invoked in parallel. Orchestration is implemented with Python’sasyncio for concurrency, while blocking RAG retrieval and model calls are isolated withasyncio.to_thread(), so that core and supporting agents can run concurrently against the single shared model without requiring separate model instances.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: To evaluate the proposed zero-trust access-control framework under controlled and repeatable conditions, we constructed a synthetic dataset of 160 access requests. The dataset was designed to capture both allowable access request and deniable access request. The dataset was organized into four equally sized groups. The first group contains 40 fully compliant requests. These requests use valid certificates, Secret-level clearance, verified multi-factor authentication, single concurrent session, verified firmware integrity, no configuration drift, and current patch status. The second group contains additional 40 compliant requests with the same access request characteristics. These two groups provide 80 samples and expectedALLOWrequests. The remaining 80 records represent deniable conditions. The third group contains 40 requests with identity and device anomaly evidences. The fourth group contains 40 requests exhibiting compromised or degraded device posture. These samples include configuration drift, outdated patches, unknown firmware integrity, reduced clearance, multiple concurrent sessions, and failed MFA verification.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: These samples include configuration drift, outdated patches, unknown firmware integrity, reduced clearance, multiple concurrent sessions, and failed MFA verification. Contextual fields included the source IP address, source zone, destination IP address, destination zone, access mode, protocol, and MQTT topic. Identity and authorization fields included certificate validity, clearance level, MFA status, role, and explicitly granted permissions. Session-related fields included the session identifier, concurrent-session count and recent anomaly count. Device-posture fields captured firmware integrity, configuration drift, and patch status. The dataset is balanced with 80 compliant and 80 noncompliant requests.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: To contextualize Agentic-ZTA’s decision quality and latency, we additionally implemented a deterministic, rule-based evaluator for the same access-control policies. The rule-based evaluator applies the identical policy set as IF-THEN conditionals without LLM inference or retrieval. Table 5 compares per-request evaluation latency for the representative use case 2 compromised-credential request under both implementations. The rule-based evaluator returns a decision in under 1 ms. The Agentic-ZTA pipeline requires approximately 45 s when only the core-agent phase is invoked, and exceeds 2 minutes when both the core and supporting phases are invoked, since agents within a phase run concurrently but the two phases execute sequentially. This latency is dominated by model inference time rather than retrieval or orchestration overhead. Table 5: Latency Comparison: Rule-Based vs. LLM-Based Agentic-ZTA Access Request.

text: LLM-Based Agentic-ZTA Access Request. Implementation Evaluation time Rule-based (deterministic) 0.0007 s LLM-based (Agentic-ZTA, core phase only) 45.67 s LLM-based (Agentic-ZTA, core+supporting phases) 134.32 s This latency gap is due to the deterministic conditional evaluator having no inference cost, while Agentic-ZTA performs LLM reasoning and retrieval at every invoked agent. Future research may focus on minimizing the model inference time. On the same 160-sample evaluation set (Section 6.4), the rule-based evaluator achieved perfect accuracy, with zero false positives and zero false negatives. Agentic-ZTA achieved 95% accuracy. Because LLM inference is non-deterministic, Agentic-ZTA cannot guarantee 100% reproducibility on identical inputs, whereas a rule-based evaluator always returns the same decision for the same input.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
section: 14 Although static rule-based access control may provide per-
text: fect accuracy on a finite rule set in less time, five reasons motivate agentic access control over it: (1) automation, (2) autonomous decision-making, (3) contextual explanations for operators, (4) the ability to address novel threats, and (5) faster policy adaptation. Automation:A rule-based evaluator only executes conditionals that an administrator has already authored. Every new policy requires manual rule-writing before the system can act on it. In Agentic-ZTA, agents evaluate access requests against retrieved policy and threat evidence without requiring a human, removing this manual step from the access-control loop. Autonomous decision-making:A rule-based access control only returns the outcome of a fixed conditional that an administrator has already authored, it does not decide anything on its own. In Agentic-ZTA agents reason over request context, retrieved policy, and threat evidence at inference time and reach an access decision autonomously, without a human.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
section: 14 Although static rule-based access control may provide per-
text: In Agentic-ZTA agents reason over request context, retrieved policy, and threat evidence at inference time and reach an access decision autonomously, without a human. Contextual explanations for operators:LLM-based agents can translate security evidence into understandable naturallanguage reasoning, reducing analyst investigation effort and improving decision transparency [46]. Agentic-ZTA records each agent’sreasoningalong with rule identifiers, preserving rule-level auditability while providing an interpretable justification. Static rules have limited ability to address novel threats: Rule-based access control systems can detect only conditions explicitly represented in their policies. When a new attack pattern appears, the system stays exposed until an administrator writes and deploys a new rule for it [47]. Agentc-ZTA can assess the semantic context of a request using retrieved policy and threat evidence, enabling risk assessment that was not present in predefined rules. Policy adaptation can be faster:Updating a rule-based system requires administrators to author, test, and deploy new rules for each policy or threat change.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
section: 14 Although static rule-based access control may provide per-
text: Policy adaptation can be faster:Updating a rule-based system requires administrators to author, test, and deploy new rules for each policy or threat change. In Agentic-ZTA, RAGgrounded agents retrieve updated policy and threat knowledge from the knowledge base at inference time. Knowledge-base update can influence subsequent assessments without modifying agent code or redeploying the orchestration layer.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
text: This paper proposes Agentic-ZTA, a multi-agent RAGenabled framework that operationalizes the NIST SP 800- 207 PDP/PEP control loop through autonomous, domainspecialized LLM agents. Trust evaluation is decomposed across agents: core agents are evaluated first, and a DENY from any core agent is enforced directly by the PEP without waiting for further agents or running trust fusion. When all core agents return ALLOW, supporting-agent assessments are combined through confidence-weighted trust fusion, so decisions are grounded in retrievable policy evidence rather than static rules. The IoBT testbed demonstrated that the framework can support diverse access-control outcomes with clear provenance. A compliant cross-zone write was permitted when all invoked agents converged above the trust threshold. A compromisedinsider read was blocked directly by a core agent’s DENY on cloned-credential evidence, without invoking trust fusion. An over-privileged cross-zone read was denied through trust fusion when the combined score fell below the acceptance threshold.

title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
text: Formal specifications are essential for deductive program verification, providing semantic abstractions for compositional verification of complex software. However, manually constructing specifications is labor-intensive, motivating automated synthesis. Despite recent advances in large language models (LLMs), existing approaches often rely on forward-only workflows and localized repair, limiting their effectiveness on real-world programs with complex dependencies among functions and loops. Verification failures may stem from previously generated specifications, causing cascading failures that local refinement cannot resolve. To address these challenges, we present SpecAgent, an agentic framework for synthesizing high-quality ACSL specifications for real-world C programs. SpecAgent integrates four components: dependency-aware planning to identify specification targets, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to provide relevant specification patterns and program context, agentic repair to diagnose defects and revisit dependent specifications, and agentic critique to assess and refine semantic strength beyond proof success. We evaluate SpecAgent on specification synthesis and program verification tasks. On 50 programs from 14 real-world repositories, SpecAgent with DeepSeek-V4 achieves 96.82% precision and 88.95% recall in synthesizing correct and strong specifications, outperforming all baselines. On 811 real-world verification targets, it successfully discharges 604, also surpassing existing baselines. These results demonstrate SpecAgent's effectiveness in synthesizing high-quality specifications and facilitating real-world program verification.

One typical approach to achieving deductive verification is based onauxiliary specifications[ 20], which are expressed in parsable, unambiguous formal languages and can abstract the behaviors of individual program structures. Specifically, loop invariants summarize the properties preserved across loop iterations, while function contracts (typically including preconditions and postconditions) characterize the behavioral guarantees of function calls.

text: This challenge has motivated substantial research into automated specification synthesis. Early approaches in this direction typically rely on heuristic rules [18, 19, 37] or machine learning techniques [31, 45, 47]. Recently, large language models (LLMs) [22, 23, 32, 38, 39, 55] have demonstrated promising capabilities in program comprehension and code summarization, bringing new light on automated program specification synthesis. A series of LLM-based approaches [11, 33, 42, 53, 54] have been explored to generate function contracts and loop invariants, often in conjunction with formal verification tools to validate and refine the generated specifications. Despite this progress, synthesizing high-quality specifications for complex real-world programs remains challenging due to fundamental limitations of existing approaches. First, they typically follow aforward-onlyworkflow, in which a specification is considered finalized once successfully generated and is not revisited in subsequent stages.

title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
text: First, they typically follow aforward-onlyworkflow, in which a specification is considered finalized once successfully generated and is not revisited in subsequent stages. Second, their repair process is predominantly localized: when verification fails, they locate and repair errors solely based on the locations indicated by the verifier, without considering specifications at other program points. These design choices become problematic in complex real-world programs, where intricate dependencies widely exist among program structures including loops and function calls, and consequently among the specifications that abstract their behaviors. Due to these dependencies, verification failure in downstream specifications may stem from semantic correctness/strength issues in other upstream specifications on which they depend. Such issues can propagate along dependency chains, triggeringcascading verification failures. However, the forward-only workflow prevents existing approaches from revisiting upstream specifications, while localized repair confines their efforts to the immediate failure site.

title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
text: However, the forward-only workflow prevents existing approaches from revisiting upstream specifications, while localized repair confines their efforts to the immediate failure site. Consequently, they may repeatedly attempt ineffective local repairs without addressing the root cause, compromising the correctness and strength of the synthesized specifications and ultimately limiting their ability to support the verification of target properties. Addressing this limitation presents several challenges. First, specification synthesis must account for dependencies induced by program structure. Real-world programs involve intricate relationships among functions, loops, and data structures, making it difficult to identify the specification synthesis order and the underlying specifications responsible for verification failures. Second, verification feedback does not directly identify the root causes of specification defects. A failed proof may result from an incorrect or insufficient specification, a runtime safety violation, or limitations of the underlying verification process. Distinguishing these causes and determining the appropriate scope of refinement require reasoning over both verification evidence and program context.

title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
text: Distinguishing these causes and determining the appropriate scope of refinement require reasoning over both verification evidence and program context. Third, proof success alone is insufficient to establish specification quality. Weak or vacuous specifications may be readily verified while failing to capture meaningful program behavior or provide useful guarantees to callers. Therefore, an effective synthesis approach must not only produce verifiable specifications but also assess their semantic adequacy and refine them when necessary. These challenges call for a shift from localized specification generation and repair towardagentic specification synthesis, where specifications are generated and refined through agentic dependencyaware decision-making. Instead of treating generated specifications as immutable artifacts, such a process can trace root causes across specification dependencies, revisit and improve defective specifications, and ensure that the resulting specifications provide meaningful behavioral abstractions beyond merely passing verification.

text: 2.1 Program Verification and Formal Specification Synthesis. Program verification [25] aims to establish whether a program satisfies desired properties, such as functional correctness and runtime safety constraints, by formally proving the consistency between program behaviors and given specifications. However, directly verifying high-level properties of complex programs is challenging due to the unbounded behaviors introduced by intricate controlflow structures, such as loops and function calls [35]. To enable effective verification, deductive verification commonly relies onauxiliary specifications[ 20], which describe the behaviors of individual program structures in precise and unambiguous formal languages. These specifications serve as semantic abstractions that allow verifiers to encode program behaviors compositionally. For example, function contracts summarize the assumptions and guarantees of function invocations, while loop invariants characterize properties preserved across loop iterations. By providing such abstractions, auxiliary specifications enable verifiers to construct local verification obligations and combine them to establish the proof for high-level properties of the overall program. , Vol. 1, No. 1, Article .

Specifically, requires statements define preconditions that must hold before function execution, ensures statements specify postconditions guaranteed after execution, and loop invariant statements describe properties maintained throughout loop iterations. These annotations provide formal behavioral summaries of program structures, which can be leveraged by verification frameworks such as Frama-C/WP [5] to generate verification conditions and discharge them using automated theorem proving and SMT solving [4, 13, 14].

title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
text: Real-world programs rarely consist of independent components. Functions interact through calls and shared data, data structures are constrained by the operations that manipulate them, and loops and their surrounding code jointly determine program states and invariants. Consequently, the specifications of individual program components are often semantically interdependent: a specification for one component often relies on preconditions, postconditions, invariants, or behavioral properties established by another. Effective specification synthesis therefore needs to account for such dependencies and propagate sufficient semantic information across them. Existing specification synthesis approaches, such as Preguss [53] and SpecSyn [34], have been aware of the phenomenon and choose to generate specifications incrementally according to the dependency relations among program components. Nevertheless, they largely follow aforward-only process: once a specification has been generated and satisfies the verification checks available at that stage, it is typically treated as finalized and will never be revisited.

text: Nevertheless, they largely follow aforward-only process: once a specification has been generated and satisfies the verification checks available at that stage, it is typically treated as finalized and will never be revisited. This creates a potential problem when an upstream specification is locally acceptable but insufficiently strong for its downstream dependents. For example, as illustrated in Figure 1, a weak but verifiable postcondition S1 (line 1) may provide insufficient semantic information for synthesizingS2 (line 4), causing semantic validity issues in the latter as well. The resulting deficiency can thus propagate along the specification dependency chain and eventually manifest as verification failures of the target properties. Confronted with such downstream failures, existing approaches typically rely on localized repair, i,e., modifying the specification at or around the observed failure location, since they are typically forward-onlyand cannot revisit finalized specifications. However, the observed failure does not necessarily indicate the actual location of the underlying defect.

In this sense, agentic synthesis naturally tackles the aforementioned deficiency propagation problem by enabling the agent to reconsider its previous decisions in light of newly acquired evidence and iteratively improve the specification set.

Upon receiving the target C program,SpecAgentuses syntax analysis to summarize relevant structural information into a deterministic program context, including function signatures, callercallee relations, and loop statement positions, before invoking the planning agent. Based on this context and direct inspection of the source code, the planning agent identifies the functions and loops that require specification instrumentation and determines the properties that should be addressed, including functional contracts and runtime safety constraints, according to the target code snippets and relevant caller/callee context. The output of the Planning Agent is a specification synthesis plan in natural language. The plan describes the intended specification targets, their designed semantics, interdependencies, and processing order. Given the target program and the current planning context, the Generation Agent constructs specifications for relevant functions and loops, including preconditions (requires), postconditions (ensures), frame conditions (assigns), loop invariants, and predicates when necessary. The generated annotations are intended to capture the behavioral and safety properties identified during the planning stage. The Generation Agent can perform search-and-replace edits [21] to instrument candidate specifications into the target code, but is constrained by the framework to specification-level modification: the agent is only allowed to add or modify ACSL annotations, without permission to modify any code implementation itself, therefore preserving the implementation semantics of the input program.

Knowledge Retrieval Based on Structural Similarity.Given a target function,SpecAgent retrieves annotated code snippets from the knowledge base according to their structural similarity to the target. The retrieval process uses a two-stage filtering and ranking procedure, progressively narrowing the candidate space from coarse structural compatibility to fine-grained similarity. This design allows the retrieved examples to share critical program characteristics with the target while avoiding unnecessary comparisons against structurally unrelated functions. • SpecAgentfirst performs a coarse-grained structural filtering using indexed attributes in the knowledge base. Specifically, functions in candidate knowledge units are required to have compatible loop structures and return types. Knowledge units that violate this criterion are excluded from subsequent computations. • The remaining candidates are further ranked according to theirJaccard Similaritytowards the target function.

text: 3.3.1 Verification Gate.Specification synthesis is not necessarily a one-shot process, since LLMgenerated specifications can be incomplete or incorrect, hindering their ability to support program verification. InSpecAgent, each synthesized specification is subjected to a verification gate before being committed to the final set of output specifications. The verification gate encapsulates Frama- C/WP [5], the verifier for ACSL, able to determine whether the candidate is syntactically valid, successfully parsed, and verifiable by the underlying verification tool. It also categorizes verification goals and outcomes reported by Frama-C/WP, including successes, syntax errors, proof failures, and timeouts, into a structured report in JSON representation, providing concrete evidence for subsequent repair. In particular, for each failure reported by the verifier, the gate maps the failure back to the source code, recovers the failure context including caller, callee, and exact source line, , Vol. 1, No. 1, Article .

This turns opaque verifier-produced information into provenance-aware repair evidence, alleviating the agent’s burden concerning error comprehension and root-cause reasoning. 3.3.2 Repairing Agent.When verification fails, aRepairing Agentis invoked to diagnose and repair the current set of candidate specifications. Given the source code and the verification report produced by the verification gate, the agent reasons about the root cause of failure and performs corresponding repair through search-and-replace edits. Typical repairs include rectifying specifications with syntax errors or non-conformance to ACSL standards, correcting inconsistent specification semantics with the target program, and strengthening the upstream specifications with weak semantic validity.

title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
text: Typical repairs include rectifying specifications with syntax errors or non-conformance to ACSL standards, correcting inconsistent specification semantics with the target program, and strengthening the upstream specifications with weak semantic validity. During diagnosis, the agent can also invoke Frama-C/WP and Frama- C/Eva [10] to obtain additional verification and value-analysis evidence, facilitating the root-cause reasoning process. After the repairing agent finishes its job, the modified candidate is submitted to the Verification Gate again. This process iterates until the candidate passes the gate or the invocation budget for the repairing agent runs out, ensuring that all committed specifications have undergone a rigorous verification process to guarantee their correctness.

text: 3.4.1 Quality Gate and Critique Agent.Verification success only establishes the consistency between the program and specifications, without guarantee that the specification is sufficientlystrong orcomplete.SpecAgenttherefore introduces aquality gateafter successful verification to assess the semantic strength of the verified specifications. Only the verified set of specifications is subjected to this assessment, since strength is meaningful only for specifications that are correct and verifiable. The Quality Gate invokes aCritique Agentto perform the semantic assessment. Given the original program, synthesis plan, set of verified specifications, and relevant editing history, the agent identifies potentially weak or missing behavioral properties, including incomplete postconditions, overly restrictive preconditions, and trivial contracts. Additionally, the agent can invoke aPostcondition Completeness Probe(detailed in Section 3.4.2) to test whether the specification sufficiently characterizes the output of a function.

title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
text: Additionally, the agent can invoke aPostcondition Completeness Probe(detailed in Section 3.4.2) to test whether the specification sufficiently characterizes the output of a function. Based on these observations, the agent eventually produces one of the following diagnosis results: •ACCEPT : The semantic strength of current candidates is acceptable, and the framework can finish with these specifications as final output. •IMPROVE : The specification exhibits localized strength deficiencies that do not involve interprocedural dependencies. The diagnosis report is thereby fed back to the Generation Agent for targeted regeneration. •REPLAN : The specification exhibits structural deficiencies that involve interprocedural dependencies and may subsequently trigger cascading strength issues. Such issues are reported to the Planning Agent, which reinitiates the synthesis process anew from the planning stage. 3.4.2 Postcondition Completeness Probe.Relying solely on LLM-based reasoning to assess whether a specification sufficiently constrains program behavior can lead to inconsistent judgments.

text: Such issues are reported to the Planning Agent, which reinitiates the synthesis process anew from the planning stage. 3.4.2 Postcondition Completeness Probe.Relying solely on LLM-based reasoning to assess whether a specification sufficiently constrains program behavior can lead to inconsistent judgments. To support the Critique Agent in assessing specification strength, we introduce thePostcondition Completeness Probeas a static analysis tool that provides stable evidence to facilitate the agent’s judgment. The majority of existing approaches for specification completeness measurement are conducted through input-output pair modification [36] or non-equivalent program mutation [17, 30], which heavily rely on the availability of representative test suites or dedicated mutation operators. Instead, we exploit a method based on the over-approximation feature of specifications [48]. , Vol. 1, No. 1, Article . Publication date: October 2026. A correct postcondition must admit all behaviors of the implementation, i.e.,B 𝑓 ⊆B 𝑆.Since𝑆may permit behaviors that are not actually exhibited by𝑓, B𝑆 is an over-approximation ofB𝑓 . A stronger postcondition constrains this over-approximation more tightly by excluding behaviors that are not permitted by the specification. In the ideal case,𝑆 precisely characterizes the function behavior (B𝑓 =B𝑆), yielding thestrongest postconditions. In this case, because a deterministic function𝑓 maps each admissible input to a unique output, such a postcondition also uniquely determines the output for every admissible input. The completeness probe checks this return-value determinacy directly through formal verification. Given a verified contract for a target function𝑓 , it constructs a temporary verification harness that invokes𝑓 twice with identical arguments, and asserts that the two return values are equal, i.e.: 𝑚:=𝑓(𝑥), 𝑛:=𝑓(𝑥),assert𝑚=𝑛.

title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
text: Given a verified contract for a target function𝑓 , it constructs a temporary verification harness that invokes𝑓 twice with identical arguments, and asserts that the two return values are equal, i.e.: 𝑚:=𝑓(𝑥), 𝑛:=𝑓(𝑥),assert𝑚=𝑛. The verifier will attempt to discharge the assertion using the target function’s contract. If the verifier proves𝑚=𝑛 , the contract is strong enough to uniquely determine the return value for each input, since the verifier cannot find another distinct output for the same input. Conversely, if both calls satisfy the contract’s preconditions but the equality cannot be proved, the postcondition admits insufficiently constrained return behavior, providing evidence of a weak return-value specification. Unlike prior works [17, 30, 36, 48, 59] that primarily stop upon a mere strength assessment result, our probe is further integrated into the agent’s iterative synthesis process through counterexampleguided refinement.

title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
text: Unlike prior works [17, 30, 36, 48, 59] that primarily stop upon a mere strength assessment result, our probe is further integrated into the agent’s iterative synthesis process through counterexampleguided refinement. When the aforementioned harness fails verification, the verifier-produced counterexamples and failed proof obligations are retained as part of the probe result and exposed to the Critique Agent. These artifacts provide concrete evidence about how the current specification fails to constrain the program behavior, facilitating the agent’s root-cause reasoning (e.g., insufficient preconditions or under-constrained return-value characterization). The Critique Agent can thereby utilize this evidence to formulate a targeted refinement rather than merely receiving a binary judgment result. In this way, the probe serves not only as a static assessment mechanism, but also as a source of counterexample-guided evidence for specification refinement.

text: Agent Behavioral Paradigm.All agents inSpecAgentoperate under the ReAct paradigm [ 58]. Specifically, each agent iteratively performs thethought-action-observationloop: in each iteration, it reasons over the currently available information, selects an appropriate action (typically a tool call), observes its outcome, and uses the obtained feedback to determine the next action. This design allows the agents to adapt their behavior (e.g., decide where to instrument specifications and what to specify) to intermediate status and results, rather than following a predefined sequential , Vol. 1, No. 1, Article . Agent Orchestrator.The agents are coordinated by a centralized orchestrator rather than agentauthored control flow to ensure the reliability of the overall framework. The orchestrator manages the workflow progress and agent invocations through a deterministic state machine following the logic shown in Fig. 2. Agents therefore operate within explicitly defined roles and responsibilities, without the capability to directly interfere with the overall workflow. The orchestrator is also responsible for controlling the computational budget. Also, the framework will be enforced to terminate and output current intermediate candidates as final results after the total number of agent invocations reaches a predefined parameter𝑁 𝑖𝑛𝑣𝑜𝑘𝑒 . Inter-agent Communication.SpecAgentsets explicit memory boundaries between agent invocations, sharing no mutable runtime state or conversation history. Instead, agents communicate exclusively through a shared workspace. Each agent invocation can access the workspace, including current specifications, verification results, and documents produced by other agents, and can in turn update relevant workspace contents that serve as inputs to subsequent agents. Consequently, agent collaboration is achieved through successive operations on this shared intermediate context.

text: We aim to answer the following research questions (RQs) through experiments: •RQ1: How is the general quality of the specifications generated bySpecAgent? •RQ2: How does each main component ofSpecAgentcontributes to its performance? •RQ3: How doesSpecAgent-generated specifications evolve with increasing agent interactions? •RQ4: CanSpecAgent-generated specifications facilitate real-world program verification tasks? 4.1 Implementation. text: RQ1&2&3.We adopt the benchmark collected by Ma et al. [ 34] to assess the general quality of the specifications produced by baselines. The benchmark contains 50 programs collected from 14 real-world repositories, all paired with verifiable ground-truth specifications to facilitate strength assessment. Programs in this benchmark yield 456.44 LoC on average, with 7 programs exceeding 1,000 LoC. Taking into consideration that the average program size in other ACSL datasets [1, 2, 11] is typically below 50 LoC, the substantial difference in program scale makes the benchmark particularly suitable for assessing the performance of baselines on real-world programs. title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
text: Following the settings of prior works [34, 59], we adopt two distinct metrics:precisionandrecall to comprehensively evaluate different aspects of specification quality. Precision measures the correctnessof the generated specifications, calculated as the percentage of correct specifications over all generated specifications. Recall assesses thestrengthof the generated specifications, measured by the percentage of ground-truth specificationscovered(i.e., there exists one generated specification that is as strong as this ground-truth) over all ground-truth specifications. We inherit the script utilized by Ma et al. [ 34] for metric calculation, which identifies equivalence between groundtruth and generated specifications by constructing a conjunctive specification that connects the two specifications with a bidirectional implication operator and verifying its correctness with Frama-C/WP. Similar practices are widely adopted in existing works [48, 59].

Trade-off between Correctness and Strength.The results further reveal a clear trade-off faced by existing methods. AutoSpec and Preguss, for example, often achieve high precision on individual repositories, but their recalls remain low, with average recall as low as 20.26% and 28.22% under DeepSeek-V4, respectively. section: 5.2 RQ2: Ablation Study on Main Components
text: We construct 4 variants ofSpecAgentby progressively augmenting a basic candidate generation process (Section 3.2) with additional agentic components. Specifically, G-only represents the basic generation process, followed by P+G that augments it with the Planning stage (Section 3.1), P+G+R further with Verification and Agentic Repairing (Section 3.3), and finally the completeSpecAgent configuration with Strength Critique and Refinement (Section 3.4). Table 3 reports the ablation results on DeepSeek-V4 and GPT-5. Overall, the results show that the individual components provide complementary benefits, while their combination is essential for achieving consistently strong performance. Using Generation alone (G only) already achieves relatively high precision, with average precision of 89.78% and 88.66% for DeepSeek-V4 and GPT-5, respectively, but its recall remains limited to 80.93% and 72.14%. Adding Planning (P+G) does not yield a consistent improvement: although recall increases slightly for DeepSeek-V4 to 83.99%, it slightly decreases for GPT-5 to 71.51%, suggesting that planning alone cannot reliably address synthesis failures.

section: 5.3 RQ3: Specification Quality Evolution over Agent Invocations
text: To investigate how specification quality evolves as agent interactions accumulate, we analyze all specification evolution trajectories at increasing numbers of agent invocations. Specifically, we vary the number of agent invocations from 2 to 10 (1 excluded since the generation stage has not yet begun) and track four metrics at each invocation count: the fraction of trajectories that have passed the verification gate, the average number of generated specifications, precision, and recall. The first metric captures how quickly trajectories reach a verification-accepted state, while the latter three characterize the quantity and quality of the resulting specifications. This analysis allows us to examine how additional agent interactions contribute to specification synthesis and whether their benefits diminish as the invocation count increases. Fig. 5 demonstrates the trend of candidate specification quality evolution as the number of agent invocations increases. As the number of agent invocations increases, candidate specification quality generally improves, but the gains gradually diminish.

text: As the number of agent invocations increases, candidate specification quality generally improves, but the gains gradually diminish. The most substantial improvement occurs in the early invocations: from 2 to 6 invocations, the mean precision increases from 93.11% to 96.32%, while the mean recall rises from 87.22% to 90.01%. Meanwhile, the average number of generated specifications increases from 79.79 to 90.70, indicating that additional agent interactions progressively expand the set of candidate specifications while maintaining or improving their quality. Beyond 6–8 invocations, however, the improvements become marginal: precision remains around 97%, recall fluctuates around 90%, and the verification-gate pass rate oscillates between 60% and 64%. These results suggest that agentic specification synthesis benefits substantially from a limited number of iterative interactions, after which additional invocations yield diminishing returns rather than continuously improving specification quality. This diminishing-return trend also justifies our choice of 10 as the maximum agent invocation budget, as further interactions are unlikely to yield substantial improvements in specification quality. Answer to RQ3:Agentic specification synthesis exhibits clear diminishing returns with increasing invocation budgets. Most improvements occur within the first 6–8 invocations, after which these metrics largely stabilize around 97% precision, 90% recall, and 60–64% verification-gate pass rate. This indicates that a moderate invocation budget is sufficient for the agent to capture most of the attainable specification quality.

section: 5.4 RQ4: Performance on Real-world Program Verification Tasks
text: To assess the practical effectiveness of the evaluated baselines on real-world software verification tasks, we evaluate all approaches on two types of real-world verification tasks. Table 4 demonstrates the number of verification targets successfully discharged by all baseline methods using DeepSeek- V4, the best-performing underlying LLM in RQ1. Overall,SpecAgentsuccessfully supports the verification of 604 out of 811 targets (74.5%), compared with 523 for Codex, 512 for Preguss, and 435 for SpecSyn. This result shows thatSpecAgentcan effectively translate program context into specifications strong enough to discharge a large fraction of verification targets. The following analysis further examines this performance across the two types of real-world verification tasks. X509-parser, Contiki, and Atomthreads.The programs are extracted from real-world repositories, with ACSL assertions on runtime error (RTE) freeness instrumented as verification targets. For these programs,SpecAgentconsistently enables the successful verification of a large fraction of the target properties. Notably, on X509-parser,SpecAgentsuccessfully discharges all 140 targets, compared with 128 and 126 for Preguss and SpecSyn, respectively.
